1    Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding
2
3    ANONYMOUS AUTHOR(S)
4
     Embedding text in one language within text of another is commonplace for numerous purposes, but usually
5
     requires tedious and error-prone “escaping” transformations on the embedded string. We propose a simple
6
     cross-language syntactic discipline, matchertext, embodied in the single rule that matchers must match –
7
     where matchers are the ASCII character pairs (), [], and {}. This discipline enables the safe embedding any
8    matchertext-compliant string into any matchertext-aware language via simple “copy-and-paste” – with no
9    escaping, obfuscation, or expansion of embedded strings. Simple string-literal syntax extensions like M"(. . . )",
10   backward-compatible with a wide variety of languages, could enable the robust embedding of arbitrary
11   matchertext strings consistently without escaping. We apply this syntactic discipline experimentally to several
12   common and frequently-embedded language syntaxes such as C-like string literals and HTML, exploring the
13   benefits, costs, and compatibility issues in adopting the proposed matchertext discipline. An empirical analysis
14   of roughly 479 million string literals drawn from thousands of production repositories finds that real-world
15
     code is already overwhelmingly compliant with this discipline, and that adopting it could eliminate around
     78% of the backslash escapes in non-binary string literals. A Go prototype passes four repositories’ tests after
16
     rewriting 14,397 of their literals. We also present MinML, an experimental markup syntax designed around
17
     matchertext, as an alternative syntax for writing HTML or XML.
18
19
20   1   Introduction
21   The need to embed valid strings in one language into valid strings in another is commonplace
22   throughout programming practice. Just a few examples include embedding regular expressions, URIs,
23   SQL queries, or HTML markup within string constants in general-purpose programming languages;
24   embedding user-entered web form data or JavaScript variables into SQL queries; JavaScript code
25   embedded in HTML via the <script> element; and URIs embedded as query strings within other
26   URIs, such as in a query to a service like the Wayback Machine.
27      An equally-ubiquitous issue arising from this practice is the need to transform the embedded
28   string – generally by escaping certain characters sensitive to the “host” language and syntactic
29   context – so that host language processors will not misinterpret embedded text as host-language text.
30   For example, the regular expression "[^"]*" matches double-quoted strings, but when embedded
31   in a C-like language must be written like re.match("\"[^\"]*\""), escaping all the embedded
32   instances of double-quote characters, so that the embedded quotes will not prematurely end the
33   string literal. Accidentally forgetting necessary escaping is naturally a common source of syntax
34   errors in manual embedding practice [17]. Automated embedding is also common practice, however,
35   such as accepting an arbitrary user-entered string on a web form and embedding it into HTML
36   via a scripting language like PHP. With automated embedding, forgetting to escape embedded
37   strings properly has become an endless source of critical security bugs such as SQL injection [11]
38   or cross-site scripting attacks [20].
39      In some future evolution of today’s standard programming languages and practices, could we
40   achieve the ability to embed any valid string in essentially any language into any other – across
41   languages – without ever having to escape, or otherwise transform or obfuscate, the string to
42   be embedded? Could we make embedding always a simple matter of verbatim “copy-and-paste”
43   when done manually, or a simple matter of concatenation or filling a “hole” in a template when
44   done automatically? We propose that the answer can and should be yes – though with important
45   challenges, costs, and caveats of course.
46      We observe that verbatim interlanguage embedding would be achievable if: (1) we could stan-
47   dardize across languages a set of open/close character pairs we will call matchers, such as the
48   parentheses (), square brackets [], and curly braces {}; and (2) we could impose the universal
49
     2                                                                                                      Anon.


50
51
52
53
54
55
56
57
58
     Fig. 1. Different languages’ escaping rules combine to increase syntactic complexity in traditional embedding
59   practice, while in matchertext only one language’s escaping rules are ever active at a given text position.
60
61
62   “syntactic discipline” that matchers must properly match in nested pairs throughout any valid string
63   – without exception – in any compliant language. If plain text is an unstructured linear sequence
64   of characters in a character set like ASCII or Unicode, then we define matchertext to be plain text
65   conforming to the additional syntactic discipline that ASCII matchers must match. For example,
66   the strings ‘(a{b}c)’ and ‘a({'}["])d’ are valid matchertext, while the strings ‘(’, ‘{a]’, ‘[(])’,
67   and ‘}{’ are plain text but are not valid matchertext.
68      Adopting the matchertext discipline does not eliminate the need for character escape sequences:
69   in fact it can slightly increase the “escaping obligations” within a language, as discussed below. But
70   matchertext enables languages to preserve the “territorial integrity” of their escaping and other
71   syntactic rules, ensuring that developers need to think about only one language’s rules at a time at
72   any given text position, even in a string composed from multiple languages. Thus, matchertext
73   arguably reduces the cognitive load of writing (or reading) cross-language embedded code. Figure 1
74   illustrates this difference with a simple example with C code embedded in HTML including the use
75   of escape codes in both languages.
76      Existing languages could be adapted incrementally to support and leverage matchertext. C-like
77   languages, for example, might adopt a new escape sequence like \[𝑚] to embed an arbitrary
78   matchertext 𝑚 into a quoted string or character literal. All characters including quotes and newlines
79   are allowed within 𝑚, provided only that matchers match. Thus, the earlier string-matching regular
80   expression "[^"]*" could be embedded into a string literal like re.match("\["[^"]*"]"). With
81   this extension, we use an escape sequence to delimit the entire embedded matchertext, but we no
82   longer need to add escape sequences within the embedded regular expression.
83      Many languages already support raw string literals in which escape sequences are disabled:
84   e.g., backtick strings like `\` in Go. A particular terminating character or sequence must still
85   be forbidden throughout the embedded text, however – in this case the backtick (`). Verbatim
86   copy-and-paste embedding remains unsafe without carefully checking the embedding text for
87   the forbidden host-language delimiters, and changing the delimiters or awkwardly rewriting the
88   embedded text (e.g., by concatenating multiple strings in different quoting styles). Matchertext, in
89   contrast, forbids no characters or sequences in embedded strings, provided only that matchers match.
90   Building on and adapting the raw-string tradition, another widely-backward-compatible approach
91   to hosting matchertext is to add support for matchertext string literals like M"(. . . )" to languages,
92   stylistically similar to the raw-string syntax R"(. . . )" already in C++. In this matchertext-literal
93   syntax, the above regular-expression example would be re.match(M"("[^"]*")").
94      To illustrate, consider a host language parsing the matchertext literal M"(print("(x)"))". On
95   reading the opener M"(, the host scans the payload print("(x)") counting matcher depth and
96   ignoring other characters, quotes and backslashes included. The sequence )" inside the payload
97   looks like the literal’s terminator, but by matcher depth, it closes the parenthesis opened before x.
98

114
115
116
117   Only the first closer that would take the depth below zero, namely the final ), ends the literal. The
118   literal’s value is the payload exactly as written, unlike the equivalent C literal "print(\"(x)\")".
119   Because the whole literal is itself matchertext, it can be pasted unchanged into another one:
120   M"(s = M"(print("(x)"))";)" holds the C statement s = M"(print("(x)"))"; with no escapes.
121   Conventional quoting needs eight backslashes ("s = \"print(\\\"(x)\\\")\";"). This benefit
122   has a cost: the payload must be matchertext. A matchertext literal cannot contain the payload
123   x)y, for example, since its lone ) would end the literal after x. Non-matchertext strings must use
124   conventional literals. Escapes like \x29 help only in conventional literals: inside M"(. . . )" the host
125   interprets no escapes, so the payload \x29 remains (and denotes) exactly those four characters.
126      It is already feasible to write code in existing languages that is also valid matchertext, with a bit
127   of care. Most languages use the matchers in structurally paired forms anyway, as in expressions
128   like a*(b+c), lists like [a,b,c], or maps like {a:1, b:"hi"}. The challenge is mainly in handling
129   the exception cases where unmatched matchers may commonly appear.
130      One traditional habit we must awkwardly unlearn in matchertext, unfortunately, is using un-
131   matched matchers in quoted strings to parse or print structured text. Clauses like printf("{") or
132   case "]" are not valid matchertext. We must therefore escape such unmatched matchers in literals,
133   as in printf("\x7B") or case "\x5D" for example. Backward-compatible language extensions
134   might ease this pain, however, with new escape sequences that include both matchers of a pair
135   but select only the pair’s opener or closer. The proposed new escape \o() represents a literal
136   open parenthesis, for example, while \c[] represents a close bracket. Table 1 summarizes a few
137   existing and proposed alternatives for escaping unmatched matchers in both C-like languages and
138   SGML-derived languages like HTML.
139      One early pragmatic experiment with matchertext is MinML [3], an alternative syntax for SGML-
140   derived markup languages such as HTML and XML. MinML uses matcher characters for structure
141   instead of matching pairs of start and end tags: e.g., em[emphasis] rather than <em>emphasis</em>.
142   Section 6 describes MinML and its tools.
143      Matchertext is a contract between text being embedded and the language receiving it. The
144   embedded string must be matchertext in the form actually inserted. The receiving language must
145   delimit it with a matchertext region, find the region’s end by matcher balance, and apply none
146   of its own escapes or restrictions inside. A balance check alone protects nothing if the receiving
147
      4                                                                                               Anon.


148   syntax still ends the value at a non-matcher such as a quote. Table 2 illustrates with SQL, using
149   a matchertext literal M'(. . . )' in a hypothetical extension to SQL. The classic injected value
150   x' OR '1'='1 contains no matchers at all, so it is valid matchertext: checking it before splicing
151   it between ordinary quotes leaves the query just as vulnerable as before. Only when SQL itself
152   delimits the value with matchers does the quote stay data, and an attempt to escape the region,
153   such as x)' OR '1'='1, fails the balance check before any query is formed. Matchertext thus
154   protects the boundary of each embedded value. What the receiving language then does with the
155   value, and which values an application should accept, remain the application’s responsibility.
156      This paper makes the following contributions:
157
             • the matchertext discipline (section 3);
158
             • backward-compatible extensions that let C-like and SGML-derived languages host matcher-
159
               text (section 4) and write embeddable matchertext conveniently (section 5);
160
             • three implementations: a CHICKEN Scheme reader extension, MinML, and Go matchertext
161
               literals tested on four repositories (section 6);
162
             • an evaluation on 479.5 million string literals from 79 organizations (section 7): excluding
163
               binary data, 98.71% are already matchertext, and matchertext literals would remove 78.05%
164
               of their backslash escapes; and
165
             • Lean 4 proofs of embeddability and of the embedding boundary (section 3.1.2).
166
167
        Although matchertext has promising security implications as table 2 illustrates, a systematic
168
      exploration of these security implications is beyond this paper’s scope and remains future work.
169
        Section 2 reviews current embedding practice, section 8 discusses related work, and section 9
170
      concludes. How matchertext affects usability and the rate of security bugs remains open (section 7.6).

172
      2     Background: needs and pitfalls of interlanguage embedding
173   The practice of embedding strings from one language into another is ubiquitous – as is the pain of
174   having to “escape” embedded strings to protect them from misinterpretation by the host-language
175   processor. This section briefly explores a few of these common existing practices and the syntactic
176   composition problems they create.
177
178   2.1    Special-purpose languages
179   Many special-purpose language syntaxes exist almost solely for embedded use in other syntactic
180   contexts. A few particularly common examples of such “little languages” include regular expressions
181   (REs), uniform resource identifiers (URIs), JavaScript Object Notation (JSON), and Structured
182   Query Language (SQL). We use REs as the running example here; section 2.4 returns to SQL, and
183   supplementary appendices F and K say more about URIs and REs.
184      Perhaps the most classic “little language” is regular expression (RE) syntax, commonly used
185   for pattern-based searches and replacements in freeform text. RE syntax traditionally uses many
186   punctuation characters for special purposes, but must also allow arbitrary embedded text to be
187   matched literally. RE syntax therefore makes heavy use of “backslash-escaping” in literal text:
188   e.g., the RE .* matches any number of arbitrary characters other than newlines, while one must
189   write \.\* to match the literal string ‘.*’. Because REs themselves are often embedded in another
190   language – frequently a C-inspired language that also uses backslash-escaping in string literals – we
191   must further backslash-escape the backslashes in RE syntax. A C string literal containing the latter
192   RE above is written "\\.\\*", for example. To match the double-backslash \\ that begins a UNC
193   name (as in \\host\path\file), the backslashes must be doubled to become \\\\ as an RE, then
194   doubled again to become "\\\\\\\\" as a C string literal containing that RE (UNC). This confusing
195   multi-level explosion of backslash escapes has been aptly dubbed leaning toothpick syndrome.
196
      Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                                    5


197   2.2   The complexity of multi-level escaping
198
      As fig. 1 illustrates, each additional level of embedding in traditional syntax adds a set of escaping
199
      requirements that the writer (or reader) of code must carefully consider and apply correctly – in
200
      the correct order – to “guide” the embedded text through the levels of host syntax that the text is
201
      embedded in. REs and C string literals each require a different set of punctuation characters to be
202
      backslash-escaped, further increasing the cognitive load when embedding. PCRE syntax helpfully
203
      promises that a backslash followed by any non-letter always “takes away any special meaning that
204
      character may have”, so one may fall back on just escaping all punctuation instead of remembering
205
      which characters must actually be escaped (PCRE). But this practice feels like a band-aid at best,
206
      and yields even more “leaning toothpicks.”
207
        The above examples also illustrate how each level of embedding can multiply the length of
208
      embedded strings by a factor of 2 or more, yielding in the worst case an exponential string-length
209
      explosion with the number of embedding levels. While more than two levels of embedding may
210
      not be that common, they do occur.
211
212
213   2.3   A proliferation of quoting conventions
214   Escaping issues such as those above have in part led many languages to support multiple different
215   types of quotes with different escaping rules. Many languages allow string literals to be either
216   single-quoted or double-quoted, so that quote characters of one type can be used literally within
217   string literals of the other, as in "'" or '"'.
218      Some languages disable escape sequences in one form of string literal so that backslashes may
219   appear literally without multiplying in number: e.g., single-quoted Bourne shell strings ('\' is the
220   same as "\\") or backtick-quoted raw string literals in Go (`\` is like "\\"). But without escapes
221   it becomes more difficult to include the forbidden terminating quote literally in the string: typically
222   one must compose multiple strings, like "it's "+'"quoted"'. Some languages such as Python
223   allow triple-quoted multiline strings to make it less likely that the terminating sequence is needed
224   in the literal: e.g., '''. . . ''' or """. . . """. But such a sequence may still need to appear, of course
225   – especially in written examples of exactly this syntax.
226      Some languages further mitigate this problem by offering an effectively-unlimited number of
227   delimiter pairs. Extended string literals in Swift, for example, surround a quoted sequence with a
228   balanced number of # signs: e.g., #". . . "#, ##". . . "##, etc. (Swift). Lua similarly offers long bracket
229   quotations like [=[. . . ]=], [==[. . . ]==], etc. (Lua). C++ supports raw-string literals of the form
230   R"𝑑(. . . )𝑑", where 𝑑 is a nearly-arbitrary delimiter string to make the opener and closer sequence
231   as unique as may be needed. This approach has the appeal that for any string to be delimited, there
232   always exists some delimiter pair that can quote it unambiguously. But the delimiters must still be
233   carefully matched to the quoted string, or vice versa. It is still not possible to embed any string of a
234   broad class verbatim into any “hole” or template in a host language without thinking about, and
235   potentially adapting, either the choice of delimiters or the embedded string. Further, the worst-case
236   “cost” of embedding in terms of string expansion still increases with each level of nesting – in this
237   case at least only linearly, rather than exponentially, in the number of levels. We would prefer,
238   however, if embedding required no expansion with increased depth.
239
240
      2.4   When security goes wrong
241
242
      The complexity of correctly embedding strings into code has created broad classes of security vulner-
243
      abilities, where untrusted (typically user-entered) strings intended for embedding can maliciously
244
      “trick” an application into interpreting parts of the string in the host language context.
245
      6                                                                                                            Anon.


246      SQL injection attacks [11], for example, typically arise from the common practice of embedding
247   user-entered strings into string literals within SQL query templates. If a server composes an
248   SQL query with a clause like "WHERE name='"+userName+"'", and the untrusted userName can
249   be maliciously crafted to contain an unescaped single quote, then the attacker can prematurely
250   terminate the SQL string literal and add other SQL clauses, like OR '1'='1' to make the clause
251   unconditionally true regardless of userName.
252      Cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks [20] similarly exploit errors in the ubiquitous practice of
253   embedding content from an untrusted source – such as fields from an HTML form – into HTML
254   or other markup without proper “sanitization” via escaping. Suppose, for example, that one user
255   of a Web-based discussion forum can post a message containing an HTML <script> tag – which
256   the discussion server then inserts into corresponding pages viewed by other users of the forum.
257   The injected JavaScript code can then potentially steal authentication cookies or other private
258   information from all users on the site who might unwittingly read the maliciously-crafted message.
259      These and other broad classes of syntactic confusion attacks have led to the security-critical
260   practice of sanitizing all potentially-untrusted user input before embedding it into security-sensitive
261   code of any kind – whether SQL queries, HTML markup, or other host languages. The forms
262   of sanitization needed in a particular context unfortunately tend to be complex and intricately
263   dependent on the syntax and semantics of the host language that the untrusted content is to be
264   embedded in. Version updates in the host language or associated libraries, which the application
265   might not always track immediately, can easily introduce new syntactic attack vectors that the
266   application has not yet countered with appropriate sanitization logic.
267      We do not expect any syntactic discipline, including matchertext, to eliminate the need to sanitize
268   untrusted inputs. If a future SQL query or Web form is designed to accept embedded matchertext
269   from an untrusted source, for example, then it will likely still be security-critical to check that the
270   untrusted content is indeed valid matchertext, and reject it if not. However, a passive verification
271   like this can be much simpler, and hence less bug-prone, than a content-modifying transformation,
272   to escape all characters or sequences that might be “sensitive” in the host language. Further, this
273   security-critical check could also be more uniform across host languages – i.e., checking only that
274   the three ASCII matcher pairs are matched correctly throughout the untrusted content, rather than
275   deeply verifying and/or transforming based on the complex syntax of a particular host language.
276   Thus, while matchertext will not eliminate the need for sanitization, it might tighten and simplify
277   the function of the most security-critical “checkpoint” – namely checking that embedding content
278   from an untrusted source preserves the structural integrity of the host language it is embedded in.
279
280   3     Matchertext design and rationale
281
      This section first defines matchertext as an abstract mathematical syntax in section 3.1, then in
282
      section 3.2 as a concrete syntactic discipline pragmatically inspired by predominant practices. These
283
      definitions represent the “core” of the matchertext concept, and are the only rules that different
284
      languages must “agree on” in order to achieve the main goal of escapeless interlanguage embedding.
285
286
287
      3.1    Abstract definition of matchertext
288   We first define abstract matchertext in order to ensure that the basic concept is clear and precise.
289      We assume at the outset we are given some arbitrary alphabet Σ, along with some finite set Π of
290   character pairs {(𝑜 1, 𝑐 1 ), . . . , (𝑜𝑘 , 𝑐𝑘 )}, such that {𝑜𝑖 , 𝑐𝑖 } ⊆ Σ for all 1 ≤ 𝑖 ≤ 𝑘. We define the openers
291   𝑂 as the set of characters 𝑜 such that some pair (𝑜, 𝑐) ∈ Π. Similarly, the closers 𝐶 are the characters
292   𝑐 such that some pair (𝑜, 𝑐) ∈ Π. We assume and require that the sets of openers and closers do
293   not overlap: i.e., 𝑂 ∩ 𝐶 = ∅. We define the matchers 𝑀 as the set of all openers and closers (i.e.,
294
      Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                               7


295   𝑀 = 𝑂 ∪ 𝐶). We define the nonmatchers 𝑁 as all characters that are not matchers (i.e., 𝑁 = Σ \ 𝑀).
296   A matchertext configuration is a pair (Σ, Π) following the above rules.
297     We now define the language 𝐿 of matchertext strings inductively (i.e., generatively) as follows:
298
           • Any string 𝑛 consisting exclusively of nonmatcher characters in 𝑁 , including the empty
299
             string, is a matchertext string in 𝐿.
300
           • For any matchertext strings 𝑚 1, 𝑚 2, 𝑚 3 in 𝐿, and for any pair (𝑜, 𝑐) ∈ Π, the concatenation
301
             𝑚 1 ||𝑜 ||𝑚 2 ||𝑐 ||𝑚 3 is also a matchertext string in 𝐿.
302
303
         Formally, 𝐿 is the Dyck Language [10] over Π where the nonmatchers are classified as neutral
304
      symbols. Equivalently, a string is matchertext if and only if it becomes a Dyck word once all the
305
      nonmatchers are removed from it. With |Π| = 1 this is the language of balanced parentheses.
306
         Intuitively, this definition captures the basic rule that matchers must match in matchertext.
307
      Openers can be introduced into valid matchertext only when paired with a matching closer, and
308
      vice versa, but nonmatchers may be interspersed throughout with no constraints.
309
         Matchertext is a purely syntactic rule. We call it a syntactic discipline rather than a language
310
      because it assigns no meaning to the strings in 𝐿 and no structure beyond the rule that matchers
311
      must match. Each matchertext-aware language defines the meaning of all characters, matchers and
312
      nonmatchers alike, and defines any further structure beyond matching of matchers.
313
      3.1.1 Escapeless embedding in matchertext. Suppose there is a set of languages L = {𝐿1, . . . , 𝐿𝑛 }
314
      whose members all agree on a common matchertext configuration (Σ, Π). Any language 𝐿ℎ ∈ L
315
      can host embedded strings in any other language 𝐿𝑒 ∈ L without escaping or other transformations
316
      to the strings from 𝐿𝑒 , provided 𝐿ℎ enforces the following simple embedding rule. Any embedded
317
      string 𝑚 ∈ 𝐿𝑒 ∩ 𝐿 must be delimited (surrounded) by some pair of strings 𝑠𝑜 , 𝑠𝑐 defined by the host
318
      language 𝐿ℎ , such that the full embedding sequence is 𝑠𝑜 ||𝑚||𝑠𝑐 in 𝐿ℎ . Further, 𝑠𝑜 must contain one
319
      or more open matchers in 𝑂 that would be unmatched in 𝑠𝑜 alone – that is, 𝑠𝑜 alone cannot be valid
320
      matchertext. Finally, 𝑠𝑐 must contain one or more corresponding close matchers in 𝐶 that would be
321
      unmatched in 𝑠𝑐 alone. For simplicity we will assume below that 𝑠𝑜 ends with an opener and that 𝑠𝑐
322
      begins with the corresponding closer, although this constraint is not strictly necessary.
323
         This embedding rule permits escapeless embedding because no fixed characters or strings,
324
      including 𝑠𝑜 and 𝑠𝑐 , need be unconditionally forbidden in the embedded string 𝑚 ∈ 𝐿𝑒 , provided
325
      that 𝑚 is valid matchertext. The host language processor need not know anything about the
326
      embedded language 𝐿𝑒 other than that 𝑚 is matchertext. A host language processor that parses
327
      left-to-right from 𝑠𝑜 can ignore any embedded instances of 𝑠𝑜 and 𝑠𝑐 within 𝑚 because the matchers
328
      they contain must match within 𝑚. The host language processor can unambiguously recognize the
329
      closer string 𝑠𝑐 that terminates the embedding because it contains at least one close matcher that
330
      would be unmatched, and thus illegal, if it were part of 𝑚.
331
         To guarantee that verbatim embedding always works, a host language must not apply transfor-
332
      mations (e.g., escapes) or restrictions (e.g., forbidden characters or sequences) within the embedded
333
      matchertext. Exceptions reduce verbatim embedding compatibility (appendix J). Operationally,
334
      after reading 𝑠𝑜 the host scans with an empty stack: each opener pushes its kind, each closer must
335
      match the top, and the first closer met with an empty stack begins 𝑠𝑐 . In M"(print("(x)"))" from
336
      section 1, the inner )" pops the ( before x and so cannot end the literal. Matcher kinds matter: the
337
      string ([)] has as many closers as openers, and no prefix has more closers than openers, but it is
338
      not matchertext, and a host language must reject it as a matchertext payload.
339
340   3.1.2 Formal guarantees. We prove two properties of the abstract language 𝐿 in the Lean 4 proof
341   assistant [12] using its Mathlib library [49], included in the lean directory of the artifact. These
342   results concern strings: they do not verify any particular compiler extension, nor the behavior
343
      8                                                                                                 Anon.


344   of the language receiving the payload. Appendix A gives the definitions and proof sketches, and
345   appendices B and C list the Lean declarations. A delimiter pair (𝑠𝑜 , 𝑠𝑐 ) is matched (definition 1) if
346   𝑠𝑜 supplies one or more openers and 𝑠𝑐 the corresponding closers in properly-nested order, with
347   nonmatchers interspersed freely, like the M and " around the parenthesis in M"(. . . )".
348
349       Theorem 1 (Always-embeddability). If 𝑚 ∈ 𝐿 and (𝑠𝑜 , 𝑠𝑐 ) is a matched delimiter pair, then
350   𝑠𝑜 ||𝑚||𝑠𝑐 ∈ 𝐿.
351
         The delimited result can thus be embedded again, to any depth, with no escaping and no expansion
352
      of the inner string, unlike the mechanisms of section 2. Let the depth of a string be its number of
353
      openers minus its number of closers.
354
355      Theorem 2 (Embedding boundary). If 𝑚 ∈ 𝐿 and 𝑐 ∈ 𝐶, then every prefix of 𝑚 has depth at least
356   0, 𝑚 has depth 0, and 𝑚||𝑐 has depth −1.
357
358      A host that has already validated 𝑚 can therefore find the start of 𝑠𝑐 as the first closer that makes
359   a depth counter negative. To validate untrusted input, the typed stack scan of section 3.1.1 decides
360   membership in 𝐿 (theorem 3 in appendix A) in 𝑂 (𝑛) time and 𝑂 (𝑑) space for nesting depth 𝑑, a
361   passive linear check rather than a content-modifying transformation.
362
363   3.2   Concrete matchertext in practice
364   The abstract definition applies to any configuration (Σ, Π), but escapeless embedding requires a set
365   of languages to agree on one. We therefore propose a standard matchertext configuration that fits
366   existing practice: its alphabet Σ is the Unicode/UCS character set [34], on which machine-readable
367   languages have already converged, and its matcher pairs Π are the ASCII parentheses (), square
368   brackets [], and curly braces {}. The matchertext discipline operates on characters, so the encoding
369   (usually UTF-8) does not matter.
370
371
      3.2.1 Standardizing on matcher pairs. A particular choice of the matcher pairs Π is less obvious,
372
      however, and hence demands more careful justification. We start by “deferring to authority”:
373
      namely the authority embodied in the UCS character set we already chose. The parentheses, square
374
      brackets, and curly braces are the only characters in the ASCII – or “Basic Latin” – code block that
375
      are standardized as members of the Open Punctuation (Ps) and Close Punctuation (Pe) character
376
      classes (Basic Latin, Ps, Pe). Exactly as their official names indicate, these character classes denote
377
      characters whose standard purpose is to serve as open and close punctuation in matched pairs.
378
        Why not the “angle brackets” <>? Many languages use < and > in pairs, for generic types in C++
379
      and Java or for markup in HTML and XML. UCS standardizes them as the less-than and greater-than
380
      symbols, however, and programs use them unmatched far more often, as in if (a < b). Requiring
381
      them to match would make inequalities cumbersome in almost all languages. Omitting <> from Π
382
      does not prevent their paired use in languages that wish to do so (sections 4.3 and 5.3); omitting
383
      them from Π merely declines to establish a universal rule that they must always match.
384
385      Why only the ASCII open/close punctuation? UCS has much more open and close punctuation, and
386   Initial Punctuation (Pi) and Final Punctuation (Pf) classes for paired quotation marks (e.g., «quote» or
387   “quote”; Pi, Pf). Machine-readable syntaxes rarely use them, partly because most keyboards cannot
388   type them directly. They also do not occur strictly in pairs: three left double quotes (U+201C, U+201E,
389   and U+201F) can match the right double quote U+201D, depending on culture and typographic
390   style. Languages may use any UCS punctuation for their own purposes, but restricting the strictly-
391   matching set Π to the ASCII matchers is simple, safe, consistent with language-design tradition.
392
      Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                                          9


393         Class    Description     Syntax               Example                                            See
394         C-like   Literal         M"(𝑚)"               M"(now quoting's "easy" in matchertext)"           4.2.1
395
                     String escape   ". . . \[𝑚]. . . "   "now \[quoting's "easy"] in matchertext"            4.2

                                     <tag attrs [𝑚]>      <code [if (a<b) { printf("some <markup>\n"); }]>
396
            ★ML      Element                                                                                 4.3.1
397                  Attribute       <tag attr=[𝑚]>       <button onclick=[show("it's done!")]>OK</button>   4.3.2
398                  Section         <![MDATA[𝑚]]>        <![MDATA[some example <b>bold</b> markup]]>        4.3.3
399                              Table 3. Summary of proposed matchertext hosting extensions.
400
401
402
        Why all three ASCII matcher pairs? All three pairs are used pervasively in different structural
403
      roles, and no obvious principle selects one of them for a global matching role. Mixing distinct
404
      pairs also offers redundancy that helps localize errors: the missing close bracket is easier to find in
405
      [{}([){}] than in [[][[][]]. Finally, every host must use some matcher pair to delimit embedded
406
      matchertext (section 3.1.1), so including all three gives languages a choice of delimiter.
407
408
      4     Host language considerations
409
      This section proposes potential extensions that let languages host embedded matchertext; section 5
410
      covers languages that wish to be embedded. The two classes of extensions are orthogonal: a language
411
      can meaningfully and justifiably adopt either set of extensions without the other.
412
413
      4.1     General hosting considerations
414
      A host language 𝐿ℎ that embeds a matchertext string 𝑚 from an arbitrary language 𝐿𝑒 follows the
415
      embedding rule of section 3.1.1: it imposes no constraint on 𝑚 other than that matchers match, and
416
      disables its own escapes and other transformations inside 𝑚. Any escaping that might be active
417
      within 𝑚 belongs to 𝐿𝑒 , not to 𝐿ℎ .
418
         A host language need not be matchertext-compliant in its own syntax. Existing languages can
419
      keep full compatibility with existing code, including allowing unmatched matchers in ordinary
420
      string literals for example, while they add extensions that host matchertext verbatim. This backward
421
      compatibility is likely essential to incremental adoption.
422
         Table 3 summarizes the extensions we propose for C-like languages (section 4.2) and SGML-
423
      derived languages (section 4.3). The same general approach also applies to URIs and regular expres-
424
      sions (see supplementary appendices F and K). These are proposals for consideration: languages
425
      need not agree on extension syntax, only on the rule that matchers match.
426
427
      4.2     C-like host languages
428
      An enormous variety of today’s popular programming languages are derived, either closely or
429
      loosely, from C [35]. Though differing widely in purpose, philosophy, and semantics, a vast number
430
      of these C-inspired languages share similar syntax for string literals. In particular, most C-derived
431
      languages use double and/or single quotes to delimit a string literal, and backslash escape codes to
432
      insert “special” characters within the literal: e.g., "hello!\n". Because quoted string literals are
433
      the primary existing syntactic mechanism for embedding (non-matchertext) strings traditionally,
434
      they represent a natural starting point for considering matchertext extensions.
435
         We propose two potential extensions to C-like languages for hosting arbitrary matchertext:
436
      matchertext literals and matchertext escapes. Any language could adopt either or both of these
437
      extensions independently.
438
439   4.2.1 Matchertext literals. A matchertext literal is a string literal whose content is entirely matcher-
440   text. We suggest allowing matchertext literals of the form M"(𝑚)", M"[𝑚]", and M"{𝑚}", where
441
      10                                                                                             Anon.


442   the substring 𝑚 is arbitrary matchertext. The content 𝑚 of such a matchertext literal must be valid
443   matchertext (matchers must match), otherwise the language processor reports a syntax error. Any
444   matchertext string may be embedded verbatim in such a literal without exceptions or escaping.
445      We could prescribe the use in this syntax of one particular matcher pair of the three, but doing
446   so seems unnecessary, since the leading M identifies the literal as hosting matchertext. The first
447   alternative using parentheses is stylistically closest to, and inspired by, C++ raw-string syntax
448   R"(. . . )". The second alternative using square brackets is stylistically more consistent with other
449   matchertext extensions we suggest such as the one below in section 4.2.2, however. We see no
450   obvious reason not to leave the choice of matcher to the user in this case.
451      The use of some matcher pair in this syntax is necessary, in any event, for hosting arbitrary
452   matchertext strings this way without escaping. The sole use of double-quotes as in M"𝑚", for
453   example, would not be fully robust or general because ASCII double quotes do not come in matched
454   pairs, as further discussed below in section 4.2.3.
455      An optional extension to this syntax could allow string interpolation within matchertext literals
456   used as templates, like M{}"(Hi {name})" or M[]"{Hi [name]}". This example would insert the
457   content of string-variable name after the prefix “Hi ”; see appendix G for details.
458      Using the upper-case M in this syntax leaves the lower-case m"𝑚" free for language-specific
459   definition, such as a hybrid variant that allows host-language escapes within the literal while also
460   enforcing the matchertext discipline, e.g., for security hardening (see appendix G.2).
461      A host language that transforms source text before tokenizing it must recognize matchertext
462   literals first, or else revert those transformations within 𝑚, as C++ raw strings already revert line
463   splices. Java’s pre-lexer translation of \u escapes would require similar handling within 𝑚.
464      A few languages currently prohibit certain characters appearing anywhere: e.g., Python prohibits
465   NUL (0) characters. NUL handling is implementation-dependent in Go and C#. Full matchertext
466   compliance requires suspending any such character prohibition within a matchertext literal. This
467   change would not affect backward compatibility, since legacy source files contain no matchertext
468   literals. Most modern languages like C++, Rust, Java, JavaScript, Swift, and Kotlin already have no
469   blanket prohibitions, as long as the source text is properly encoded (usually UTF-8).
470
471   4.2.2 Matchertext escapes in ordinary string literals. Given the ubiquity of backslash-escaped
472   string literals in C-like languages, another potential extension for hosting matchertext in such
473   languages is via a new escape sequence usable within ordinary string literals, such as \[𝑚], where
474   𝑚 is arbitrary matchertext. The embedded matchertext 𝑚 is uninterpreted by the host language
475   processor except to verify that ASCII matchers match and to find the terminating close bracket.
476   Thus, quote characters, backslashes, whitespace, newlines, or other control codes cease being
477   “special” within the matchertext 𝑚 – at least from the perspective of the host language. For example,
478   the string literal "\["'\]" becomes equivalent to "\"\'\\" using conventional escaping. These
479   and other characters might of course be “special” with respect to whatever embedded language 𝑚
480   might be written in.
481      Embedding matchertext in a string literal via a new escape sequence has the advantage that the
482   entire literal need not be matchertext. Literals can mix matchertext with conventional literal text
483   including host-language escape sequences: e.g., "\t\[let's indent]\n\t\[a "quote"]".
484      The choice of square brackets for the proposed matchertext escape sequence is somewhat
485   arbitrary: we could instead use parentheses or curly braces, or a longer sequence such as \m[𝑚].
486   Any choice may conflict with existing syntax in some language: e.g., \(𝑚) conflicts with string
487   interpolation in Swift [4], \[𝑚] conflicts with the current handling of unrecognized escapes
488   in Python, JavaScript, and C [16, 44], and \{𝑚} conflicts with Unicode escapes in Ceylon [37].
489   Fortunately, different languages need not agree on the precise syntax for hosting matchertext
490
      Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                                 11


491   (a) Embedding strings in other languages as element content in HTML
492        HTML <code>printf("Example &lt;b&gt;bold&lt;/b&gt; and &amp;bigstar; reference in HTML");</code>
493          +M <code [printf("Example <b>bold</b> and &bigstar; reference in HTML");]>
           HTML <script>document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "a <" + "/script> end tag";</script>
494
             +M <script [document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "a </script> end tag";]>
495
496   (b) Embedding strings in other languages within element attributes in HTML
497        HTML <button onclick="emitCharacter('\'')">Emit Apostrophe</button>
498          +M <button onclick=[emitCharacter("'")]>Emit Apostrophe</button>
499
      (c) Embedding strings within CDATA (character data) sections in XHTML
500       XHTML <code>example <![CDATA[<![CDATA[character data]]]]><![CDATA[>]]> markup</code>
501          +M <code>example <![MDATA[<![CDATA[character data]]>]]> markup</code>
502       XHTML <code>example <![CDATA[<![CDATA[<![CDATA[double embedded]]]]]]>
503               <![CDATA[><![CDATA[>]]]]><![CDATA[>]]> markup</code>
             +M <code>example <![MDATA[<![MDATA[<![MDATA[double embedded]]>]]>]]> markup</code>
504
505
506
      Fig. 2. Example embedded strings in ★ML languages, standard versus proposed matchertext extensions (+M).
507
508
      strings, and can choose whatever syntax best suits that particular language. To fulfill matchertext’s
509
      main objective, different languages need to agree only on the basic rule that the embedded string
510
      itself is arbitrary except that ASCII matchers must match.
511
512   4.2.3 Other alternatives. Other obvious alternatives seem less suitable. Quotes cannot delimit
513   embedded matchertext: the ASCII quotes " and ' do not come in pairs, and Unicode quote pairing
514   depends on culture (section 3.2.1), so the matchertext rule alone cannot locate the end of the string.
515   ASCII matchers alone, or combinations such as ["𝑚"] or "[𝑚]", conflict with existing constructs
516   such as grouping a*(b+c), lists [a,b], maps {a=1}, a singleton list ["x"], or a string "[x]".
517
518   4.3   SGML-style markup host languages
519   While the venerable Standard General Markup Languages (SGML) [23, 33] itself has waned in
520   popularity, its derivatives HTML [51] and XML [53] are now ubiquitous in Web content and
521   programming. Wherever the differences between these markup languages are not important, we
522   will refer to them all as ★ML languages.
523      In their basic role as markup languages used to produce rich, structured documents, ★ML
524   languages frequently play “host” to embedded strings in countless other languages: typically, in
525   the language(s) of software or APIs that a marked-up document is written about. Embedding code
526   in other languages as verbatim text is a basic and frequently-used purpose of HTML’s <code> and
527   <pre> tags, for example. Beyond merely marking up verbatim text in other languages, however,
528   HTML in particular has evolved to include special-purpose support for embedding several other
529   languages within HTML: namely scripting languages such as JavaScript or Tcl, cascading style
530   sheets (CSS) [56], MathML [54], and SVG [55].
531      The ★ML languages are surprisingly complex syntactically, especially given their simple-sounding
532   purpose of “merely” describing structured markup of usually human-readable text. In particular,
533   there are at least three different syntactic contexts in which strings in other languages are often
534   embedded into ★ML languages – and in which three different sets of quoting and escaping rules
535   apply. Strings are often embedded (1) as the content of an element, (2) as an attribute within an
536   element’s start tag, or (3) as verbatim text within a CDATA section. We address each of these
537   syntactic contexts in turn, in each case suggesting potential matchertext extensions that could help
538   mitigate the various forms of “escaping hell” that these embedding contexts can create.
539
      12                                                                                              Anon.


540   4.3.1 Strings embedded as element content. One common form of embedding into ★ML is marked-
541   up text serving as the content of an element: e.g., example code between <code> and </code>
542   tags or between <pre> and </pre> tags in HTML. Further, the <script> and <style> tags in
543   HTML exist specifically to embed scripting language code and cascading style sheet (CSS) code,
544   respectively, as their content.
545      The syntactic rules governing what can appear in text embedded as element content, however,
546   depend intricately on the tag, the ★ML language in question, and even the language version. In
547   most elements such as <code> and <pre>, any characters < and & appearing in the embedded string
548   must be escaped (as &lt; and &amp;), to prevent the ★ML parser misinterpreting them as the
549   start of a tag or a character reference, respectively. In XML, this rule applies to the content of all
550   elements, including the content of <script> and <style> tags of XML-based XHTML. In HTML,
551   however, the content of <script> and <style> tags is raw character data, uninterpreted by the
552   HTML parser except to find the end tag. The content of such tags therefore can contain unescaped
553   < and & characters – and cannot use HTML character entity references for escaping. In all of these
554   cases, figuring out what must be, what can be, and what cannot be escaped is subtle and potentially
555   confusing.
556      As a potential extension enabling any of the ★ML languages to host embedded matchertext
557   conveniently, we suggest the following new element syntax:
558                                  <name attributes [matchertext content]>
559
         The name and attributes are the tag name and optional attributes as they normally appear in a
560
      start tag, and matchertext content is the element content as literal matchertext enclosed in square
561
      brackets, uninterpreted except to find the end by matching matchers. This syntax represents the
562
      entire element, with no end tag, so it is more concise than traditional start/end tag pairs. Since the
563
      content within brackets is uninterpreted except to match matchers, the content cannot contain
564
      further markup (child elements) or ★ML character entity references when using this syntax.
         Figure 2(a) illustrates a few examples of embedding code into a <code> or <script> element,
565
566
      either in standard HTML or with the proposed matchertext content syntax (+M). The first example
567
      embeds literal HTML markup within HTML. The second illustrates the more troublesome case where
      embedded JavaScript wishes to output a </script> end tag within a string literal. Since HTML
568

      entity references are unavailable within a <script> element, the code must either use JavaScript
569

      escapes, or construct the </script> tag from two string literals, to prevent the embedded literal
570

      from prematurely ending the <script> element. In matchertext content syntax, neither example is
571
572
      problematic and both are more concise.
573
574   4.3.2 Strings embedded as attribute values. Besides element content, scripting language code is
575   often embedded in the attribute values of ★ML start tags, most commonly to handle events in
576   active user interface elements. Attribute values represent a different syntactic context in which
577   different escaping rules apply. When attribute values are delimited with single or double quotes, the
578   quote character that introduced the value must be escaped (as &apos; or &quot;) if it is embedded
579   in the attribute value. Character references may appear and are substituted in attribute values,
580   like normal elements such as <code> in HTML but unlike <script> or <style> content. As the
581   HTML specification notes, this means that script and style data cannot be simply cut-and-pasted
582   between element content and attribute values without care for the changed escaping rules [52,
583   App. B.3.2]. HTML forgivingly allows < and “unambiguous” & characters to appear unescaped in
584   attribute values, while XML requires them to be escaped (along with the active quote character).
585      One potential matchertext hosting extension would be simply to allow square brackets as a third
586   “quoting style” for attribute values, where the text between the brackets is uninterpreted except
587   to match matchers and find the end. With this extension as well as that above, the quoting and
588
      Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                               13


589   escaping rules for matchertext element content and matchertext attribute values would be identical,
590   allowing code to be cut-and-pasted between these contexts freely.
591      Figure 2(b) illustrates script text embedded in attribute values, without and with matchertext
592   hosting extensions. The example illustrates how any time a string literal is needed in such embedded
593   text, the embedding effectively “consumes” both quote characters in standard HTML or XHTML.
594   Matchertext embedding, in contrast, preserves JavaScript’s “syntactic freedom” of using one quote
595   character to quote a verbatim instance of the other.
596      A legacy HTML5 tokenizer reads <code [ as an attribute name ending at the first >, and attr=[
597   as an unquoted value; a sanitizer and a browser that disagree on the syntax enable mutation
598   XSS [27], so every processor of such a document must parse the extensions.
599
600
      4.3.3 Strings embedded in CDATA sections. SGML and XML (but not HTML) also embed strings in
601
      CDATA sections <![CDATA[text]]>, which disallow only the terminator ]]> within text. Because no
602
      escapes are available inside them, however, a ]]> in the embedded text forces awkward contortions:
603
      the usual fix replaces it with ]]]]><![CDATA[> to close and reopen the section. This happens
604
      whenever one writes about CDATA sections in ★ML markup.
605
         We suggest a matchertext section form <![MDATA[matchertext]]>. Figure 2(c) compares CDATA
606
      and MDATA sections. The first example shows how MDATA sections remove the ]]> problem,
607
      provided that matchers match. The second shows “double embedding”, where CDATA sections
608
      become unreadable while MDATA sections nest with no difficulty.
609
610
      5     Embedded syntax considerations
611   Having focused above on host language considerations, we now switch focus to considerations for
612   languages to be embedded as matchertext. The languages of interest for embedding overlap heavily
613   with those of interest as host languages; we separate these discussions mainly to emphasize the
614   orthogonality of host- and embedded-language issues and cleanly separate them.
615      It is already entirely feasible to write valid matchertext in most of the languages we will consider
616   for embedding. This is because most popular machine-readable languages already largely conform
617   to the “matchers must match” rule in their explicit uses of the matcher characters. Violations of the
618   matchertext rule most commonly occur only in embedded “free-form” text such as string literals
619   and comments. The language extensions we will propose are motivated almost exclusively by
620   increasing convenience and visual clarity, and are by no means essential.
621
622   5.1    String literals in C-like languages
623   Almost certainly the most common context in which unmatched matchers appear in most of today’s
624   existing source code is within string literals. This is especially true of code designed to print, or
625   parse, machine-readable code in almost any syntax. Structured pretty-printing code frequently
626   includes code sequences like this:
627
               print("[")
628
               output all elements of a list
629
               print("]")
630
631
       Similarly, parsing code often uses if, switch, or case conditionals to recognize and parse
632
      matcher-delimited syntactic structures, as in:
633            if peekNextChar() == '[':
634              scanChar('[')
635              scan all elements of a list
636              scanChar(']')
637
      14                                                                                               Anon.


638      Printing and scanning code like this generally violates the matchertext rule, and adapting such
639   code most likely represents the biggest “pain point” in any venture to write readily-embeddable
640   matchertext.
641      Almost all programming languages already offer a workable if slightly cumbersome solution:
642   simply replace unmatched matchers in string literals with suitable numeric character escapes. In-
643   stead of print("["), for example, write print("\x5B") (C, C++, JavaScript) or print("\u005B")
644   (Java, JavaScript, Go). This always works; the main annoyance is that it requires the writer (and
645   reader) of the code to remember or look up the codes for the matcher characters in an ASCII table.
646      The usual solution in C-like languages to handle “special” characters in string literals is simply
647   to backslash-escape the special character, like \[. This traditional solution does not work for
648   unmatched matchers in matchertext, however, because the matchertext rule is deliberately language-
649   independent and oblivious to language-specific syntax such as that of string literals. So a backslash-
650   escaped unmatched bracket \[ remains just as much a matchertext violation as the bracket alone.
651      The escapes proposed in section 1 avoid ASCII tables: each contains both matchers of a pair,
652   properly matched, and selects only the opener or closer, as in \o() or \c[] (table 1).
653      The choice of the letters o and c to escape the matchers is consistent with their standardized
654   character classes: “Open Punctuation (Ps)” and “Close Punctuation (Pe)”, respectively (Ps, Pe). We
655   might consider l and r for “left” and “right”, except \r is a near-universal escape for carriage
656   return (CR). A few languages already use o or c in escape sequences: e.g., Raku uses \o[𝑛] to
657   denote the ASCII character with octal value 𝑛, and uses \c[𝑛] to denote a Unicode character with
658   name or decimal value 𝑛. Many of these existing uses are technically not in conflict syntactically,
659   provided the existing use requires a non-empty string between the matchers – as Raku does in the
660   above cases, for example. JavaScript, however, already reads "\o()" as "o()". In any case, different
661   languages need not agree on specific escape sequences for unmatched matchers and are free to
662   make their own stylistic choices.
663
664   5.2   Comments and derived documentation
665
      Another context in which unmatched matchers may regularly appear in typical source code is
666
      within comments: e.g., as part of human-readable text describing how the associated code handles
667
      particular characters. Conventional language processors usually just ignore unmatched matchers
668
      (along with everything else) in a comment. But the matchertext discipline operates below and
669
      oblivious to the syntax of a particular language, and hence does not know what a “comment” is –
670
      so the matchertext discipline must disallow unmatched matchers even in comments.
671
         Since comments are generally intended for humans reading the source code, it is usually possible
672
      simply to rephrase the comment to avoid a literal use of unmatched matcher characters: e.g., just
673
      name it (‘open parenthesis’) instead of writing it (‘(’). Another alternative, if a language adopts the
674
      above extensions for string literals, is simply to use these matchertext-friendly escapes in comments
      as well (e.g., \o()).
675
676
         In some languages, comments often get used to produce API documentation, using tools like
677
      Javadoc or godoc. In such cases, it may be useful to interpret escape sequences such as those above
678
      while auto-generating documentation from source code, so that a documentation comment like
      ‘// Parse a \o()’ becomes ‘Parse a (’ in the formatted output generated from the code.
679
680
681
682
      5.3   SGML-derived languages
683   Considerations similar to those above for string literals apply when we wish to embed ★ML-
684   language markup into other languages as matchertext. The most common reason unmatched
685   matchers appear in markup is when needed in literal text being marked up: e.g., human-readable
686
      Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                               15


687   text about the matcher characters or syntactic constructs built from them, or code examples that
688   contain unmatched matchers.
689      As with C-style string literals, ★ML languages already offer a workaround: simply use character
690   references, either named (like &lpar;) or numeric (&#x0028;). For the same reasons as above, we
691   may like to have extensions offering more visually-obvious alternatives for writing matchertext:
692   e.g., &(<); and &(>); for open and close parentheses (table 1).
693      Appendices F.3 and K.1 discuss embedding URIs and regular expressions as matchertext.
694
695   6     Implementations of matchertext
696
      This section describes three implementations of matchertext: a reader extension for CHICKEN
697
      Scheme, matchertext literals in the Go toolchain, and MinML, a matchertext-based markup syntax.
698
699
      6.1    Matchertext for CHICKEN Scheme
700
701
      The matchertext egg for CHICKEN Scheme [47] adds the matchertext literals of section 4.2.1
702
      as a reader extension (appendix H gives a grammar). Since CHICKEN Scheme is not a C-style
703
      language, the M prefix is rewritten as #M to use the language’s reader’s dispatch character. The #M
704
      prefix has no prior meaning in the language, so the extension is conservative for the same reason
705
      as in C-like languages. So #M"(\([{}]))" converts to the string \([{}]) without escapes, and
706
      #M{}"({greeting}, world)" interpolates the Scheme expression greeting into the literal. The
707
      egg currently accepts only parentheses around the literal’s content.
708
709
      6.2    Matchertext literals in Go
710   A 128-line patch adds the literals of section 4.2.1 to the Go toolchain; M" is a syntax error in Go
711   today, so no valid program changes. We ran the tests of four corpus repositories with stock Go, with
712   patched Go, and with patched Go after rewriting the 14,397 literals whose value M"(. . . )" holds
713   verbatim. All 242 packages with tests passed in every run, and the rewritten literals’ toothpicks fell
714   from 37,662 to 88 (appendix I).
715
716   6.3    MinML: minified matchertext markup
717   One early experiment in matchertext-friendly syntax design is MinML [3], an alternative syntax
718   for SGML-derived markup languages like HTML and XML.
719      Beyond merely adding matchertext hosting and embedding extensions as discussed in the sections
720   above, MinML more ambitiously reformulates the basic ★ML syntax to rely on matching brackets
721   for basic structure rather than matching start/end tags as in SGML tradition. For example, emphasis
722   is written like em[emphasis] rather than <em>emphasis</em>. Character references are written
723   like [star] instead of &star;.
724      A “quotation” delimited by matching quote characters may be written like "[quotation]
725   in MinML instead of &ldquo;quotation&rdquo;. A comment is -[comment] instead of
726   <!--comment-->. A raw embedded text sequence is written +[verbatim] instead of
727   <![CDATA[verbatim]]>. MinML’s embedded sequences leverage matchertext to support
728   arbitrary nesting, so a verbatim example of a raw matchertext sequence is simply +[+[example]],
729   rather than in XML:
730
                                     <![CDATA[<![CDATA[example]]]]><![CDATA[>]]>
731
732     For escaping unmatched matchers, MinML supports both the traditional HTML named and
733   numeric character references, and bracket-delimited versions of the “visual” matcher escapes
734   suggested in table 1 and in appendix K.1.1 for regular expressions:
735
      16                                                                                                Anon.


736                                    Matchers           Open Close
737                                    Parentheses () [(<)] [(>)]
738                                    Brackets      [] [[<]] [[>]]
739                                    Braces        {} [{<}] [{>}]
740      MinML tools include a Go library and command-line tool that convert MinML to HTML or XML
741   (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/matchertext-D61C/go/matchertext), an extension to the Hugo
742   static website generator, a Language Server Protocol server with diagnostics, hover, and completion
743   for Visual Studio Code, JetBrains IDEs, and five other editors (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/
744   matchertext-D61C/dev/vscode/minml-preview), and a pandoc extension that converts to and from
745   MinML (ANONYMIZED).
746
747   7 Evaluation
748
      To ground the matchertext discipline in evidence rather than argument, we evaluate it on a large
749
      corpus of real-world code. The evaluation treats every string literal and comment in the corpus as
750
      a candidate embedded string, and answers four questions that source code can answer directly:
751
752
            Q1 How matchertext-compliant is existing code? (section 7.2)
753
            Q2 Which embedded languages carry the violations? (section 7.3)
754
            Q3 How much escaping would matchertext remove? (section 7.4)
755
            Q4 How deeply does embedding nest in practice? (section 7.5)
756   Section 7.6 discusses the questions the corpus cannot answer.
757
758   7.1     Methodology
759   The analysis extracts embedded text directly from each language’s own lexical structure rather
760   than from ad-hoc pattern matching. For C and C++ it uses the Clang lexer [39, 48], recognizing
761   all string-literal forms (including the wide, UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32, and raw variants) and both
762   comment styles; for the remaining languages it uses in-process tree-sitter grammars [8]. Both paths
763   emit string-literal and comment samples that feed the same metric computation. Each candidate
764   string is further classified by content – e.g., as a URI, regular expression, HTML, SQL, or shell
765   fragment – using deterministic structural detectors backed by a trigram naive-Bayes model, with
766   an explicit Unknown bucket for samples too short or ambiguous to label safely. The compliance and
767   escaping metrics below do not depend on this classification, which affects only the per-category
768   attribution of results.
769      The corpus is drawn from GitHub and is intended to represent mature, widely-deployed pro-
770   duction code: every non-archived repository of 79 organizations behind operating-system kernels,
771   databases, browsers, language toolchains, and similar infrastructure. It comprises 13,702 repositories
772   and roughly 13.08 million source files (on the order of 1.5 TiB of code), yielding approximately
773   479.5 million string-literal samples and 297.4 million comment samples. Exact duplicates (forks,
774   vendored copies) are 40.4% of files, with 35.7% of string samples. JavaScript alone contributes about
775   191 million string samples, reflecting both its prevalence and its string-heavy style.
776      The key metrics are as follows. A sample is matchertext-compliant when its ASCII matchers
777   match (section 3), and the compliance rate is the fraction of compliant samples; a strict rule treats a
778   wrong-kind closer (e.g., ) closing [) as a violation, while a relaxed rule permits it. A violation is one
779   unmatched or wrong-kind matcher. A toothpick is a single backslash character in a sample, following
780   the term “leaning toothpick syndrome” of section 2. To estimate the escaping that matchertext
781   would remove, each compliant string literal is rewritten as the equivalent escapeless C++ raw string
782   literal R"(. . . )" (same toothpicks as M"(. . . )") and the surviving backslashes are counted, yielding
783   a toothpick reduction. The rewrite decodes every escape, \x5B included, and drops its backslash
784
      Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                                   17


785                               Stream                  Samples   Compliant     Compliant
786                                                                    (strict)    (relaxed)
787                               String literals         479.5 M      98.71%             —
                                  Comments                297.4 M      96.54%        96.57%
788
                                  Files (all fragments)   13.08 M      86.55%        86.68%
789
      Table 4. Matchertext compliance rate and sample size by stream, under the strict and relaxed rules (relaxed
790
      measured for comments and files only). A file complies when all its literals and comments do.
791
792
793
794   unless it decodes to one or to a control other than tab, LF, or CR, which is kept verbatim. An
795   escape that cannot be written raw, such as a non-UTF-8 byte, keeps its backslash too, as does every
796   escape of a literal whose decoded content is not matchertext. Binary-data literals (BinaryData and
797   PseudoBinaryData, such as file headers, test vectors, or terminal codes) are out of scope: they are
798   not readable text, writing their byte escapes raw would break the encoding, and their brackets are
799   byte values, not delimiters. They count only toward sample and toothpick totals. Finally, nesting
800   depth is the deepest matcher nesting a sample reaches; raw depth also counts unclosed openers.
801
802   7.2   Q1: Compliance of existing code
803   Existing code is already highly matchertext-compliant at the level of individual embedded fragments.
804   As table 4 shows, 98.71% of in-scope string-literal samples and 96.54% of comment samples are
805   compliant as written. Per file, counting all its literals and comments, compliance is lower, 86.55%,
806   because one violating fragment makes the whole file non-compliant, so per-sample-rare violations
807   still touch a noticeable fraction of files. As whole source texts, 94.65% of files are matchertext; 89,138
808   files comply fragment by fragment but not as a whole (e.g., '['), and 1,149,620 the reverse (e.g., "["
809   . . . "]"). The relaxed rule barely changes any of these figures (file compliance rises only to 86.68%,
810   comments to 96.57%), which means almost all violations are genuinely unmatched matchers rather
811   than correctly-paired-but-wrong-kind nesting. Compliance is also high across every host language,
812   with string-literal compliance staying within a narrow band from 96.62% for the least-compliant
813   language up to 99.93%, so no language in the corpus is broadly non-compliant.
814
815   7.3   Q2: Where violations concentrate
816   Violations are far from evenly spread across embedded-language categories. As table 5 shows,
817   regular expressions and shell fragments carry 645,675 and 322,074 violations respectively, despite
818   making up only 0.4% and 1.2% of classified samples; relative to their sample counts they are far more
819   often non-compliant than prose or identifiers. CSS is similarly disproportionate, contributing 133,909
820   violations from only 3,198,385 samples. By contrast, identifier-like tokens and URLs are essentially
821   violation-free. The pattern is that unmatched matchers cluster in exactly the categories whose
822   syntax routinely uses brackets singly, rather than in the bulk categories (plain prose, identifiers,
823   file paths) that dominate the sample count.
824      This is the pain point we anticipate in section 5.1: printing and parsing code that emits or
825   matches lone, unmatched matchers within string literals – e.g., print("[") or case "]" – is where
826   the matchertext discipline bites. Resolving the data by host language separates two effects. The
827   first is the per-sample violation rate: the bracket-single-use categories are most violation-prone
828   wherever they appear, and acutely in JavaScript, where regular expressions average 0.66 violations
829   per sample, shell fragments 0.10, and CSS 0.05. The second is absolute contribution, which is partly
830   volume-driven: in every major host but Swift the largest source of violations is strings of a single
831   character or of punctuation alone, such as "[" (61.0% of C++’s violations and 62.8% of Java’s), and
832   ordinary prose still causes 15.4% and 20.8%, not because prose is error-prone – its rate is only about
833
      18                                                                                                      Anon.


834         Category          Share   Samples    Violations   Toothpicks    Category           Toothpicks    Share
835
            PlainText         42.1%    192.0 M      627,916    97,066,295   PlainText           97,066,295   36.7%
            IdentifierLike    28.5%    130.2 M      205,437       183,406   BinaryData          57,492,023   21.7%
836
            SingleCharacter    8.0%     36.3 M    1,815,933     4,066,837   PseudoBinaryData    35,490,129   13.4%
837         FilePath           4.5%     20.4 M       15,884       867,358   PseudoURL           11,689,784    4.4%
838         FormatString       2.9%     13.2 M      283,057     5,718,577   Regex                9,030,097    3.4%
839         Punctuation        2.2%      9.9 M    1,591,921     3,447,446   JSON                 6,949,509    2.6%

            Shell              1.2%      5.7 M      322,074     1,820,281   FormatString         5,718,577    2.2%
            CSS                0.7%      3.2 M      133,909     2,044,427   HTML                 4,797,354    1.8%

            Regex              0.4%      2.0 M      645,675     9,030,097   SingleCharacter      4,066,837    1.5%
