844
845   Table 5. Largest embedded-string categories by share of the 456.3 M classified string samples (95% of all),
846
      with their samples, violations and toothpicks; numbers, empty strings, and categories below 1% other than
      CSS and regular expressions are omitted. Unknown holds the unclassified samples. (b) ranks by toothpicks,
847
      as a share of all string-literal toothpicks.
848
849
850
851   0.01 – but because prose strings are so numerous. The categories most likely to violate are thus
852   consistent across hosts.
853      Most string literals are not cross-language embeddings at all: plain prose, identifier-like tokens,
854   and file paths account for about 75% of classified samples (table 5). Among the languages that
855   motivate our injection discussion, SQL accounts for 0.19%, JSON for 0.09%, CSS for 0.70%, and XML
856   for 0.12%. Because the corpus is infrastructure-heavy (section 7.1), these figures likely understate
857   web-facing combinations such as SQL in application code or HTML templating. The classification
858   is content-based and best-effort, so its finer categories are approximate, and it shows what is
859   embedded, not why.
860
861   7.4     Q3: Escape reduction
862   The central benefit of matchertext is the escaping it removes. Rewriting each compliant string
863   literal as an equivalent C++ raw string literal eliminates 78.05% of the in-scope toothpicks (71.09%
864   deduplicated), cutting them from about 171.5 million to about 37.6 million. Of those left, 40% are in
865   non-compliant literals, which are not rewritten; the rest are mostly backslashes a raw literal still
866   holds: escaped ones as in regular expressions (12%), those of literals already raw (6%) or opening a
867   Swift interpolation (0.4%), and control characters kept verbatim (38%). Escaped binary data, out of
868   scope, holds another 93.0 million. The host’s raw-string form could hold 81.2% of the compliant
869   literals, and only a matchertext literal the other 18.7% (e.g., C and Java lack raw strings); both counts
870   include literals without escapes. As a concrete case, the compliant C++ regular-expression literal
871   "\\b,\"axis\":(\\d+)\\b" carries eight toothpicks; rewritten verbatim as the matchertext literal
872   M"(\b,"axis":(\d+)\b)", the two quote escapes and three doubled backslashes vanish and only
873   the three genuine backslash escapes remain – a 62.5% reduction in that one literal.
874      The reduction is large but content-dependent. Across the 79 organizations it ranges from 23.17%
875   to 97.86%, with half of them between 64% and 85%. As table 6 (appendix E) shows, it also varies
876   by host language: C-family languages and Java see most of their toothpicks eliminated (C 79.99%,
877   C++ 85.50%, Java 73.92%), while others reduce much less, most strikingly Swift (30.29%), Python
878   (30.85%), and TypeScript (36.92%).
879      A notable finding is that compliance and escape relief are largely independent, turning on where
880   a language’s escaping actually lives. TypeScript is the clearest case: its string literals are 99.74%
881   compliant, among the highest in the corpus, yet rewriting them removes only 36.92% of their
882
      Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                             19


883   toothpicks, among the lowest. The reason is that most of its backslashes (56.4%) sit in regular
884   expressions, whose own escapes, like the three in the example above, survive the rewriting. A
885   language can therefore satisfy the matchertext rule almost everywhere and still gain little from
886   raw-string rewriting: the cost of becoming compliant and the benefit of doing so are distinct
887   quantities.
888
889   7.5    Q4: Nested embedding
890   Most bracket nesting is shallow. Most samples contain no matchers at all, and depth falls off
891   sharply beyond one: the average per-sample maximum depth is only 0.097 for string literals and
892   0.275 for comments. Deep nesting does occur in a heavy tail – the single deepest string sample
893   reaches a raw depth of 41,066, in C++ (though that literal’s deepest matched nesting is at most 500),
894   followed by maxima in C# (3,757), Python (1,195), and PHP (773) – but such cases are vanishingly
895   rare. Comments nest more on average than string literals, consistent with comments containing
896   structured examples and prose, whereas string literals more often hold a single flat fragment. For
897   reference, appendix D plots the full depth distribution.
898
899   7.6    Discussion and open questions
900   The results suggest that the adoption cost is small and the benefit could be large. Over 98% of
901   string literals and over 96% of comments need no change, and rewriting the compliant majority
902   as raw string literals or matchertext literals would remove 78.05% of the in-scope toothpicks. The
903   remaining violations fall where section 5 predicts, in syntaxes that use brackets singly, and the
904   near-identical strict and relaxed comment rates suggest that they are lone matchers, the case the
905   escapes of table 1 address, rather than closers of the wrong kind. Two questions from section 1
906   remain open: how matchertext affects usability in common embedding tasks, such as editing HTTP
907   or SQL queries, and how it affects the rate of syntax-related and security-related bugs, which a
908   static corpus analysis cannot measure. Nor is the corpus a random sample: it counts forks and
909   vendored, generated, or minified files without deduplication, so widely copied code weighs more.
910
911   8     Related Work
912   The theory of syntactic structures, such as regular and context-free languages [10] or parsing
913   expression grammars [21], has already been richly developed. Nothing about the matchertext
914   discipline is particularly new or technically challenging from a formal language perspective. The
915   Dyck language [10] already covers much of the discipline: matchertext is a Dyck language with
916   neutral symbols (section 3.1). In addition, every context-free language is a homomorphic image of
917   a Dyck language filtered by a regular language [10]. Matchertext keeps brackets visible, making it a
918   visibly pushdown language [2, 42], so a host can find where embedded text ends without parsing it.
919      However, less prior work has focused on the ubiquitous practice of syntactically embedding
920   strings of one language into those of another, or addressing the practical challenges this embedding
921   creates.
922      Some prior work has focused on developing better tooling to support string-embedding practices
923   as they currently stand: e.g., parsing regular approximations of string-embedded languages [50], and
924   support in integrated development environments [25] and static analysis tools [36]. This work does
925   not attempt to explore syntax design practices that could make languages more cleanly embeddable
926   in the first place, however.
927      Other work prevents injection attacks by preserving the syntactic structure of the embedding.
928   Su and Wassermann [46] define a command injection attack as input that changes the intended
929   syntactic structure of a generated query or document. They mark each input substring with meta-
930   characters and parse the result with an augmented grammar that rejects inputs that do not form
931
      20                                                                                               Anon.


932   a complete syntactic unit. Bravenboer et al. [7] embed the grammar of a guest language such as
933   SQL into a host language such as Java, and generate code that applies the necessary escaping
934   automatically. Both approaches need the grammar of the embedded language. Matchertext preserves
935   structure without any embedded-language grammar: the host language checks only that untrusted
936   content is matchertext (appendix A.2), and needs no escaping.
937      Significantly more work has focused on domain specific embedded languages or DSELs [31],
938   particularly in the functional programming community. DSELs build upon the syntax and semantics
939   of a general-purpose programming language such as Haskell, and thus benefit from – but also
940   become dependent upon and specialized to – the syntax, semantics, and tooling of the host language.
941   DSELs are thus unsuitable for embedded languages that wish to remain agnostic to, or usable across
942   a variety of, host languages. Asking an embedded language to conform only to the matchertext
943   discipline is a much more lightweight proposition than asking the embedded language to adopt,
944   and become usable only with, the entirety of Haskell or another general-purpose language.
945      Pragmatically, some existing languages come close to the matchertext approach to embedding.
946   Strings in PostScript [1] are delimited by matching parentheses, and may contain unescaped literal
947   parentheses provided they are balanced. The dc calculator [30] similarly delimits strings with
948   brackets, and allows balanced nested brackets. Link syntax in Markdown, like [text](url), allows
949   brackets within text and parentheses within url provided they are balanced [40]. Balanced delimiters
950   also nest within Tcl braces, Perl’s q{. . . }, Ruby’s %q(. . . ), and m4 quotes. These languages balance
951   only their own delimiter, however, and do not support general cross-language embedding. TEX
952   groups and Scribble @-expressions balance braces [19, 38], though TEX skips escaped \{ that
953   matchertext counts; Rust token trees and Honu [45] balance brackets only after lexing; SDF, Silver,
954   and Eco [14, 26, 57] need the guest’s grammar, and quasiquoters [41] host-specific quotes.
955      Closest to matchertext, Wyvern’s type-specific languages [43] delimit generic literals with curly
956   braces, square brackets, or angle brackets, and require only that the delimiter characters inside
957   the literal body be balanced. The type expected at the literal’s position selects the logic that parses
958   the body. Wyvern thus also finds the end of a literal by bracket balance alone, without parsing its
959   content. Its rule applies only within Wyvern, however, and only to the delimiter in use, whereas
960   matchertext asks every compliant language to balance all three ASCII matcher pairs, so that any
961   matchertext string embeds verbatim in any matchertext-aware host.
962
963   9 Conclusion
964   Matchertext is a syntactic discipline that enables the verbatim embedding of strings across languages
965   with no transformation or expansion, by enforcing only the single rule that the ASCII matchers –
966   parentheses, square brackets, and curly braces – must always appear strictly in matched pairs. We de-
967   velop the basic principles and rationale for matchertext, and explore potential backward-compatible
968   extensions to existing classes of languages both to host embedded matchertext strings, and to
969   write embeddable matchertext conveniently. Lean 4 proofs establish that embedding preserves
970   matchertext and that a host finds the end of an embedding by matcher balance alone. Excluding
971   binary data, 98.71% of 479.5 million string literals are already matchertext, and matchertext literals
972   would remove 78.05% of their backslash escapes. MinML shows that a full markup syntax can rest
973   on the discipline. Its effect on usability and on the rate of injection bugs remains open for future
974   work.
975
976   AI Use
977   We used Claude Code (Anthropic) to write the Python content classifier of the evaluation (sec-
978   tion 7.1), to optimize parts of the source-code analyzer, to write the script that fetches the corpus
979   repositories from GitHub, and to figure out quirks when learning and writing Lean 4 proofs.

       The artifact, available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/matchertext-D61C/, comprises the

       Lean 4 proofs of the embeddability and boundary results (appendices B and C), the Go library
984
       and command-line tool that converts MinML to HTML or XML, a patch that adds matchertext
985
       literals to the Go toolchain, with the script that rewrites the string literals of four Go repositories
986
       as matchertext literals and runs their tests before and after, and its results, and the source-code
987
       analyzer and corpus-collection scripts used in the evaluation (section 7), together with the analyzer’s
988
       raw results. The corpus itself (about 1.5 TiB) is not included; the scripts rebuild it by cloning the
989
       repositories, whose later changes can cause small differences from the numbers reported here. We
990
       will submit the artifact to Artifact Evaluation.

1128   A     Formal results
1129
       This appendix details the formal results summarized in section 3.1.2. Theorems 1 and 2 are mecha-
1130
       nized in Lean 4 (appendices B and C); theorem 3 has a paper proof only.
1131
1132   A.1     Always-embeddability
1133
       Two closure properties of 𝐿 do the work:
1134
1135        Lemma 1 (Concatenation closure). If 𝑎 ∈ 𝐿 and 𝑏 ∈ 𝐿, then 𝑎||𝑏 ∈ 𝐿.
1136
            Lemma 2 (Wrapping). If 𝑚 ∈ 𝐿 and (𝑜, 𝑐) ∈ Π, then 𝑜 ||𝑚||𝑐 ∈ 𝐿.
1137
1138     Concatenation follows by induction on the derivation of 𝐿, and wrapping directly from the
1139   nesting rule (details in appendix B).
1140     To capture the shape of the delimiter strings 𝑠𝑜 , 𝑠𝑐 that practical hosts use, we define a matched
1141   delimiter pair inductively:
1142
         Definition 1 (Matched delimiter pair). The pair (𝑠𝑜 , 𝑠𝑐 ) is matched if it can be formed by these
1143
       rules:
             • (𝑜, 𝑐) is matched for every (𝑜, 𝑐) ∈ Π;
1144

             • if (𝑠𝑜 , 𝑠𝑐 ) is matched and (𝑜, 𝑐) ∈ Π, then (𝑜 ||𝑠𝑜 , 𝑠𝑐 ||𝑐) is matched; and
1145
1146
             • if (𝑠𝑜 , 𝑠𝑐 ) is matched and 𝑥 ∈ 𝑁 is a nonmatcher, then both (𝑥 ||𝑠𝑜 , 𝑠𝑐 ) and (𝑠𝑜 , 𝑠𝑐 ||𝑥) are
1147
               matched.
1148
1149     Intuitively, 𝑠𝑜 supplies one or more open matchers and 𝑠𝑐 the corresponding close matchers in
1150   properly-nested order, with nonmatcher characters interspersed freely except next to 𝑚, exactly
1151   the shape of practical delimiters such as the M and " surrounding the parenthesis in M"(. . . )".
1152
          Proof sketch of theorem 1. By induction on the derivation that (𝑠𝑜 , 𝑠𝑐 ) is matched (defini-
1153
       tion 1). The base case wraps 𝑚 using lemma 2, and a matcher step likewise wraps the induction
1154
       hypothesis; a nonmatcher step prepends or appends a single-character nonmatcher string (which
1155
       is in 𝐿 by the flat rule) using lemma 1.                                                      □
1156
1157     Theorem 1 establishes the compositional core of escapeless embedding: for any valid matchertext
1158   𝑚, with no exceptions, the delimited result 𝑠𝑜 ||𝑚||𝑠𝑐 is itself valid matchertext. It can therefore
1159   be embedded again, to any depth, with no escaping and no expansion of the inner string, the
1160   property that distinguishes matchertext from the quoting and escaping mechanisms surveyed in
1161   section 2. The complementary claim of section 3.1.1, that a host parser scanning left-to-right can
1162   unambiguously locate the terminating 𝑠𝑐 , follows from the same balanced structure; appendix A.3
1163   makes it operational and theorem 2 mechanizes it.
1164
1165   A.2     Deciding matchertext
1166   Whereas theorem 1 shows that embedding produces valid matchertext, a host language, or a check-
1167   point guarding against untrusted input (section 2), must also be able to recognize it. Membership in
1168   the language 𝐿 of section 3.1 is decided by a single linear scan, shown as Algorithm 1. The stack
1169   holds the openers seen so far that are not yet matched; each closer must pop the opener of its own
1170   pair, and the string is matchertext exactly when the scan finishes with an empty stack.
1171
          Theorem 3 (Correctness of Verify). For every string 𝑠, Algorithm 1 returns true if and only if
1172
       𝑠 ∈ 𝐿.
1173
1174     Proof sketch. By induction on the scan, the stack holds exactly the currently unmatched
1175   openers, so Verify rejects exactly the unmatched or mismatched matchers.                □
1176
       Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                                25


1177   Algorithm 1 Deciding whether a string 𝑠 is matchertext.
1178
        1: function Verify(𝑠)
1179
        2:    𝑠𝑡 ← empty stack                                                         ⊲ unmatched openers
1180
        3:    for each character 𝑥 in 𝑠 do
1181
        4:        if 𝑥 ∈ 𝑂 then push 𝑥 onto 𝑠𝑡
1182
        5:        else if 𝑥 ∈ 𝐶 then
1183
        6:            if 𝑠𝑡 is empty or (Top(𝑠𝑡), 𝑥) ∉ Π then return false
1184
        7:            pop 𝑠𝑡
1185
        8:      return whether 𝑠𝑡 is empty
1186
1187
1188
          The procedure runs in 𝑂 (𝑛) time and 𝑂 (𝑑) space on an input of length 𝑛 with maximum nesting
1189
       depth 𝑑, which section 7.5 finds is almost always tiny. This is the concrete basis for the security
1190
       argument of section 2: admitting untrusted embedded content requires only this passive linear check,
1191
       rather than a content-modifying transformation that must anticipate every sequence sensitive to
1192
       the host language. It is also exactly the check that our empirical analysis (section 7) applies to every
1193
       string literal and comment in the corpus.
1194
1195   A.3    Locating the end of an embedding
1196
       A host must also find where an embedding 𝑠𝑜 ||𝑚||𝑠𝑐 ends without being misled by matchers inside 𝑚.
1197
       A host language that has already validated 𝑚 as matchertext, for example because 𝑚 was produced
1198
       by the process in theorem 1, can scan the text after 𝑠𝑜 with a depth counter starting at 0 and stop at
1199
       the first closer that makes the depth negative. By theorem 2 this is the first character of 𝑠𝑐 , which
1200
       definition 1 makes a closer. A host language reading untrusted input, by contrast, must instead use
1201
       the typed stack of Algorithm 1, since a depth counter alone accepts wrong-kind pairs such as ([)].
1202
       The host must then check that the complete 𝑠𝑐 follows.
1203
1204   B     Machine-checked: always-embeddability
1205
       The declaration heads below summarize the Lean 4 development that establishes theorem 1 (there
1206
       named embedding_closed_under_context). lean/core.lean holds the definitions, faithful to the
1207
       abstract definitions of section 3.1, and lean/always_embeddable.lean holds the proof. The
1208
       disjointness of openers and closers assumed there (𝑂 ∩ 𝐶 = ∅) appears as the premise hdisj; tactic
1209
       proof bodies are elided and given in full in the source files.
1210
       -- lean/core.lean
1211
       import Mathlib
1212
1213   variable {𝛼 : Type*}         -- the alphabet
       variable (Pi : Set (𝛼 × 𝛼 )) -- the set of pairs
1214
1215   def Opener     (x : 𝛼 ) : Prop := ∃ y, (x, y) ∈ Pi
1216   def Closer     (x : 𝛼 ) : Prop := ∃ y, (y, x) ∈ Pi
       def Matcher    (x : 𝛼 ) : Prop := Opener Pi x ∨ Closer Pi x
1217
       def Nonmatcher (x : 𝛼 ) : Prop := ¬ Matcher Pi x
1218
1219   -- Lemma: no character is both an opener and a closer.
       theorem disjoint (h : ∀ x y z, (x, y) ∈ Pi → (z, x) ∈ Pi → False)
1220
           (x : 𝛼 ) : ¬ (Opener Pi x ∧ Closer Pi x) := by ...
1221
1222   -- The language of matchertext strings,
       -- one constructor per clause of the inductive definition.
1223
       inductive MT (Pi : Set (𝛼 × 𝛼 )) : List 𝛼 → Prop where
1224     | flat (n : List 𝛼 ) (h : ∀ x ∈ n, Nonmatcher Pi x) : MT Pi n
1225
       26                                                                                                                Anon.


1226     | nest (m1 m2 m3 : List 𝛼 ) (o c : 𝛼 ) (hp : (o, c) ∈ Pi)
1227            (h1 : MT Pi m1 ) (h2 : MT Pi m2 ) (h3 : MT Pi m3 ) :
             MT Pi (m1 ++ [o] ++ m2 ++ [c] ++ m3 )
1228
1229   -- lean/always_embeddable.lean
1230   import core

1231
       -- Lemma: the empty string is matchertext.
1232   theorem mt_nil : MT Pi ([] : List 𝛼 ) := by ...
1233
       -- Lemma: the language is closed under concatenation.
1234
       theorem mt_append {a b : List 𝛼 } (ha : MT Pi a) (hb : MT Pi b) :
1235       MT Pi (a ++ b) := by ...
1236
       -- Lemma: wrapping a matchertext string in a single matched pair.
1237
       theorem mt_wrap {m : List 𝛼 } (hm : MT Pi m) {o c : 𝛼 } (hp : (o, c) ∈ Pi) :
1238       MT Pi ([o] ++ m ++ [c]) := by ...
1239
       -- Matched delimiter contexts: nested matcher pairs
1240
       -- with nonmatchers interspersed freely on either side.
1241   inductive AllMatch (Pi : Set (𝛼 × 𝛼 )) :
1242       List 𝛼 → List 𝛼 → Prop where
         | pair (o c : 𝛼 ) (hp : (o, c) ∈ Pi) : AllMatch Pi [o] [c]
1243
         | cons (o c : 𝛼 ) (s_o' s_c' : List 𝛼 ) (hp : (o, c) ∈ Pi)
1244            (rest : AllMatch Pi s_o' s_c') :
1245         AllMatch Pi (o :: s_o') (s_c' ++ [c])
         | nonmatch_o (x : 𝛼 ) (s_o' s_c' : List 𝛼 ) (hx : Nonmatcher Pi x)
1246
                (rest : AllMatch Pi s_o' s_c') :
1247         AllMatch Pi (x :: s_o') s_c'
1248     | nonmatch_c (y : 𝛼 ) (s_o' s_c' : List 𝛼 ) (hy : Nonmatcher Pi y)
                (rest : AllMatch Pi s_o' s_c') :
1249
             AllMatch Pi s_o' (s_c' ++ [y])
1250
1251   -- Theorem (always-embeddability): embedding a matchertext
       -- string in a matched context always yields matchertext.
1252
       theorem embedding_closed_under_context
1253       (hdisj : ∀ x y z, (x, y) ∈ Pi → (z, x) ∈ Pi → False)
1254       {m : List 𝛼 } (hm : MT Pi m)
           {s_o s_c : List 𝛼 } (hs : AllMatch Pi s_o s_c) :
1255
           MT Pi (s_o ++ m ++ s_c) := by ...
1256
1257
            Proof sketches of the lemmas.
1258
1259      Proof sketch of lemma 1. By induction on the derivation of 𝑎 ∈ 𝐿. If 𝑎 is a string of nonmatch-
1260   ers, a second induction on the derivation of 𝑏 ∈ 𝐿 either extends that nonmatcher string, when 𝑏 is
1261   also flat, or splits off the outermost matched pair of 𝑏 and reattaches 𝑎 on its left via the nesting
1262   rule. If 𝑎 itself has the form 𝑎 1 ||𝑜 ||𝑎 2 ||𝑐 ||𝑎 3 , then 𝑎||𝑏 = 𝑎 1 ||𝑜 ||𝑎 2 ||𝑐 ||(𝑎 3 ||𝑏), which lies in 𝐿 by the
1263   induction hypothesis on 𝑎 3 and one application of the nesting rule.                                                     □
1264
1265     Proof sketch of lemma 2. Immediate from the nesting rule of section 3.1 with 𝑚 1 and 𝑚 3 both
1266   empty and 𝑚 2 = 𝑚.                                                                            □
1267
1268   C     Machine-checked: embedding boundary
1269   The declaration heads below summarize the Lean 4 development in lean/embed_boundary.lean
1270   that establishes theorem 2 (there named embed_boundary), extending the closure development
1271   of appendix B with the boundary characterization that closure alone does not supply. It reuses
1272   the definitions Opener, Closer, and MT and the premise hdisj of appendix B, imported from
1273   lean/core.lean. Tactic proof bodies are elided here and given in full in the source file.
1274
       Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                                 27


1275   import core
1276
       open Classical
1277
1278   variable {𝛼 : Type*}         -- the alphabet Σ, kept abstract
1279   variable (Pi : Set (𝛼 × 𝛼 )) -- the set of pairs Π

1280
       -- Net matcher depth: +1 per opener, -1 per closer, 0 per nonmatcher. Noncomputable since only
1281   -- a host-language implementation would need a computable version.
1282   noncomputable def delta (x : 𝛼 ) : Int := if Opener Pi x then 1 else if Closer Pi x then -1 else 0
       noncomputable def depth (l : List 𝛼 ) : Int := (l.map (delta Pi)).sum
1283
1284   -- Lemma: depth is additive over concatenation.
1285   theorem depth_append (a b : List 𝛼 ) : depth Pi (a ++ b) = depth Pi a + depth Pi b := by ...

1286
       -- Lemma: one character's contribution.
1287   theorem depth_singleton (x : 𝛼 ) :
1288       depth Pi [x] = (if Opener Pi x then 1 else if Closer Pi x then -1 else 0) := by ...

1289
       -- Lemma (balanced): a matchertext string has net depth 0, since it is well balanced.
1290   theorem depth_zero
1291       (hdisj : ∀ x y z, (x, y) ∈ Pi → (z, x) ∈ Pi → False)
           {m : List 𝛼 } (hm : MT Pi m) : depth Pi m = 0 := by ...
1292
1293   -- Lemma (floor, the crux): no prefix of a matchertext string dips below depth 0, so
1294   -- a reader tracking matcher balance never underflows inside the embedding.
       theorem depth_prefix_nonneg
1295
           (hdisj : ∀ x y z, (x, y) ∈ Pi → (z, x) ∈ Pi → False)
1296       {m : List 𝛼 } (hm : MT Pi m) :
1297       ∀ p, p <+: m → 0 ≤ depth Pi p := by ...
1298
       -- Theorem (embedding boundary): placing a matchertext value m in a hole closed by c and reading to
1299   -- balance recovers exactly m: every prefix of m stays at depth ≥ 0, m itself returns
1300   -- to 0, and c is the first character to drive the depth negative, so the balance
       -- boundary is precisely |m|. It follows from the three lemmas above: the boundary
1301
       -- result is a corollary, not new machinery.
1302   theorem embed_boundary
1303       (hdisj : ∀ x y z, (x, y) ∈ Pi → (z, x) ∈ Pi → False)
           {m : List 𝛼 } (hm : MT Pi m) {c : 𝛼 } (hc : Closer Pi c) :
1304
           ( ∀ p, p <+: m → 0 ≤ depth Pi p)
1305          ∧ depth Pi m = 0
1306          ∧ depth Pi (m ++ [c]) = -1 := by ...
1307
1308
       D    Nesting-depth distribution
1309
1310
       Figure 3 plots the full distribution of the nesting depths summarized in section 7.5, for string literals
1311
       and comments on log–log axes. It shows the sharp fall-off after depth one and the long, sparse tail.
1312
       E   Per-host-language statistics
1313
1314   F   Uniform Resource Identifiers
1315   Uniform resource identifier (URI) syntax [5] has become a ubiquitous notation for naming and
1316   locating not only web pages but innumerable other Internet resources. As a “small” special-purpose
1317   syntax, as opposed to a general-purpose programming language, it is arguably more often useful as
1318   an embedded rather than a host syntax, as we will focus on later in appendix F.3. In practice, however,
1319   innumerable other identifier syntaxes get embedded into URIs regularly, either as scheme-specific
1320   text (e.g., file names, phone numbers, cryptographic hashes), or even as query parameter values.
1321   This common and intentional use of URI syntax as a uniform “wrapper” for other identifier syntaxes
1322   makes URIs worth careful consideration as a potential host syntax for matchertext embedding.
1323

                                    Rust              51             8.6 M      99.23%       68.90%         120
1357
                                    OCaml             18             433 k      96.62%       76.14%          23
1358
       Table 6. Per-host-language statistics for selected languages: contributing organizations, string-sample count,
1359
       string-literal compliance rate, toothpick reduction, and the deepest raw matcher nesting observed in any
1360
       single sample. OCaml is shown as the least-compliant host language in the corpus.
1361
1362
1363
1364      We suggest two syntactic extensions to host matchertext within URIs, which are potentially
1365   complementary and could be adopted either together or individually.
1366      First, extending the existing “percent-encoding” scheme for escaping special characters (e.g.,
1367   %20 to represent an ASCII space), we suggest matchertext escape sequences of the form %[𝑚]. Like
1368   the backslash-escape form \[𝑚] suggested in section 4.2 for C-like languages, the matchertext
1369   𝑚 is uninterpreted by the URI processor other than to verify that matchers match and find the
1370   terminating close bracket. For example, file:///%[a<b>c`d] becomes a valid URI usable to access
1371   a local file named a<b>c`d, containing characters typically allowed in Unix-derived file systems but
1372
       Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                             29


1373                  URI   http://dev.site/myLibrary/doc/genericContainer%3CT%3E/api/
1374                  +M    http://dev.site/myLibrary/doc/%[genericContainer<T>]/api/
                      URI   http://search.engine/linksto?site=http%3A%2F%2Fmy.site%2F&results=50
1375
                      +M    http://search.engine/linksto?site=%[http://my.site/]&results=50
1376
                      URI   http://calculator.site/?expr=(1%2B2)*3%5E4%2F5
1377                  +M    http://calculator.site/?expr=%[(1+2)*3^4/5]
1378
1379                Fig. 4. Examples of URIs without and with matchertext hosting extensions (+M).
1380
1381
1382   traditionally forbidden in URIs. Since percent-encoding by the host URI processor is disabled within
1383   the embedded matchertext 𝑚, %[100%] becomes valid and equivalent to 100%25. In effect, this
1384   matchertext escape syntax offers a more concise, less obfuscated way to express arbitrary portions
1385   of URIs in which several characters would otherwise have to be individually percent-encoded.
1386   Figure 4 shows a few examples of URIs using conventional and matchertext percent-escapes for
1387   comparison.
1388      Another potential syntactic extension is to allow square-bracketed sequences [𝑚] to appear
1389   verbatim within the URI body, where 𝑚 is otherwise-uninterpreted matchertext. This is not an
1390   escape sequence: the square brackets are not eliminated in URI processing, so [@] is equivalent to
1391   %5B%40%5D. This extension essentially serves as a matchertext-friendly quoting syntax that may be
1392   used in specific URI schemes, or within pathname components or query strings, to embed substrings
1393   in other identifier syntaxes (even other URIs) without obfuscation. We will explore the usefulness
1394   of this extension further when we consider matchertext resource identifier or MRI syntax later in
1395   appendix F.3.3. This extension is backwards-compatible with existing (valid) URIs because current
1396   syntax permits brackets only in special-purpose IPv6 address syntax as part of the authority field.
1397
1398   F.1   Precedents for URI syntax extensions
1399   Originally standardized as uniform resource locators or URLs [6], URIs traditionally allow only a
1400   small subset of ASCII characters to appear verbatim. Non-graphical characters, or those deemed
1401   “unsafe” for various reasons, must be escaped via percent-encoding. The set of allowed characters,
1402   and their purposes, has been “liberalized” multiple times historically, however.
1403      IP version 6 introduced colon-separated hexadecimal addresses (e.g., 1234::abcd [29]), which
1404   conflicted with the URI’s use of the colon to separate an IP address from a port number (e.g.,
1405   http://1.2.3.4:80/). The square brackets [] were therefore shifted from forbidden to “reserved”
1406   characters in URIs, for use only in embedding IPv6 addresses into the “authority” field of URIs, like
1407   http://[1234::abcd]:80/ [28].
1408      International Resource Identifiers or IRIs [15] further liberalized URI syntax, allow most of the
1409   graphical characters in the extended Unicode/UCS character sets to appear verbatim in URIs. IRIs
1410   preserved backwards compatibility in part by defining standard conversion processes back and
1411   forth between internationalized IRIs and legacy ASCII-only URIs. The set of ASCII characters
1412   allowed in IRIs remained tightly restricted, however.
1413      Still later, IPv6 introduced scoped identifier syntax, allowing an interface number or name to be
1414   specified with an IPv6 address, e.g., 1234::abcd%1 or 1234::abcd%if0 [13]. This new syntax again
1415   conflicted with URI syntax, leading to further syntactic hacks involving mandatory percent-escaping
1416   of the percent sign indicating a scoped identifier [9].
1417      These points in URI evolution illustrate a repeating precedent for liberalizing URI syntax to
1418   accept previously-forbidden characters and to make URIs more “friendly” and accommodating of
1419   embedded strings derived from other languages – whether machine-readable (e.g., IPv6 addresses)
1420   or human-readable (international languages). Adopting matchertext hosting extensions such as
1421
       30                                                                                                    Anon.


1422   those above, permitting URIs to host other syntaxes more cleanly without the traditional syntactic
1423   hacks and percent-encoding obfuscation, could be a useful step in allowing URIs to fulfill their
1424   ambition of being a uniform “meta-syntax” framework accommodating an unlimited variety of
1425   specific identifier syntaxes.
1426
1427   F.2   How liberal to liberalize?
1428   The above considerations, however, raise the obvious question: how far should liberalization of URI
1429   syntax go? Beyond the square brackets, which other characters that were previously disallowed in
1430   URIs and IRIs should eventually be permitted, and in what contexts?
1431      In terms of our current focus on hosting embedded matchertext, the ideal would clearly be to allow
1432   any UCS characters in URIs – at least within a matchertext escape %[𝑚] or a matchertext quote
1433   [𝑚]. This approach would clearly provide the maximum latitude for embedding other syntaxes
1434   into URIs cleanly in the future. Further, only this “extreme liberalization” would guarantee that any
1435   matchertext, from any language conforming to the standard matchertext configuration (section 3.2),
1436   may be embedded verbatim into a URI without escaping.
1437      As appendix J discusses, however, this arguably might be “going too far” in the case of URIs.
1438   We first consider the graphical ASCII characters that are currently disallowed in URIs, then the
1439   non-graphical characters such as spaces and control codes.
1440
1441      Graphical characters: URIs traditionally forbid “angle brackets” <> and double quotes " from use
1442   within URIs, because these characters are sometimes used to delimit URIs in surrounding freeform
1443   text: e.g., <http://my.site/> or "http://my.site/". In any “legacy” URI parsing context un-
1444   aware of matchertext extensions, the appearance of these characters within a URI might indeed
1445   prematurely terminate the recognized URI, an issue we will return to later in appendix F.3.2. In a
1446   context aware of the matchertext extensions, however, there is no syntactic ambiguity between
1447   angle-brackets or double-quotes used to surround a whole URI and any that may appear within
1448   embedded matchertext. The matchers delimiting the embedded matchertext unambiguously serve
1449   to differentiate “inside” from “outside”: e.g., as in <http://my.site/%[>"<]>.
1450      The original URL standard in 1994 [6] additionally declared all the following characters to be
1451   “unsafe” in URIs “because gateways and other transport agents are known to sometimes modify
1452   such characters”:
1453                                             { } | \ ^ ~ [ ] `
1454
          More than 30 years later, the “gateways and other transport agents” that text containing URIs
1455
       tend to pass through have no doubt evolved drastically (or been replaced entirely). It is far from clear,
1456
       therefore, that URIs today face the same modification perils as those of 1994. The text justifying the
1457
       exclusion of these characters was dropped from the latest URI standard [5], though the characters
1458
       themselves remain forbidden apart from the square brackets. IRIs introduced thousands of other
1459
       new characters into the allowed set without dire consequences. With adequate care taken for
1460
       backwards compatibility (as was done with IRIs), it may be high time to consider allowing the rest
1461
       of the ASCII printing characters above into URIs – at least in embedded matchertext hosted within
1462
       URIs.
1463
1464      Non-graphical characters: URIs also traditionally disallow non-graphical characters such as
1465   spaces, as well as control characters such as newlines and tabs, for a different purpose: the goal of
1466   transcribability. It was difficult in 1994 to transcribe by hand a string containing spaces, newlines,
1467   tabs, or other control codes, and it is probably just as difficult to do so today. In an era of proliferating
1468   QR codes, the only question might be to what extent manual transcribability is still a crucial goal
1469   for URIs.
1470
       Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                                   31


1471      Nevertheless, manual transcription remains an important and not-uncommon use of URIs, and
1472   compromising the transcribability goal would arguably represent a much more fundamental shift
1473   in the principles underlying URIs than decisions about allowing or disallowing particular printing
1474   characters. This consideration therefore suggests that we cease the liberalization of URIs just short
1475   of allowing non-graphical characters.
1476      Further, the transcribability goal is served only if the entire URI is readily transcribable, including
1477   any embedded matchertext substrings it may contain. Thus, as appendix J.1 mentions, the URI
1478   context may justify a tightened matchertext configuration whose alphabet Σ is reduced to exclude
1479   non-graphical characters. The cost is that arbitrary matchertext is not necessarily copyable verbatim
1480   from C-like languages into URIs, but this compatibility cost may be justified in this case.
1481
1482   F.3    Embedding Uniform resource identifiers
1483   Since uniform resource identifier (URI) syntax represents a special-purpose “little language” just
1484   for expressing identifiers, URIs are predominately embedded in other contexts – software source
1485   code, documentation markup, configuration files, etc. Especially since URIs are intended to be
1486   human-readable, it would thus seem useful if URIs could be maximally “friendly” for embedding.
1487
1488
       F.3.1 The near-matchertext-compliance of URIs. Conventional URI syntax [5] already “nearly”
1489
       complies with the “matchers must match” rule and is thus, usually, embeddable verbatim in a
1490
       matchertext context. Curly braces are formally disallowed in URIs. Square brackets are allowed
1491
       only to surround IPv6 addresses in the authority field, in properly-matched fashion. Thus, the
1492
       only unmatched matchers that can exist in a strictly-valid URI are parentheses. Even these, when
1493
       appearing in URIs, often still come in matched pairs anyway.1
1494
          In the rare cases when unmatched parentheses are “needed” in a URI, they may always be
1495
       percent-escaped as %28 or %29. For example, the string ‘open(’ becomes ‘open%28’ in a matchertext
1496
       URI, ‘close)’ becomes ‘close%29’, and ‘close)open(’ becomes ‘close%29open%28’. The string
1497
       ‘open(close)’ need not be rewritten at all in a matchertext URI, since the matchers it contains
1498
       already happen to match.
1499
          We could always consider escaping extensions such as %o() and %c(), but it is far from clear that
1500
       their likely-marginal need would justify the syntactic complexity in this case. Even if URI syntax is
1501
       liberalized further to allow square brackets and/or curly braces in components, it is unclear how
1502
       commonly unmatched matchers would be needed, since it is not particularly common to write
1503
       parsing or scanning code within a URI for example.
1504   F.3.2 The URI end-finding problem. Nevertheless, URI syntax does suffer from at least one signif-
1505   icant usability flaw arising from its frequent use as an embedded syntax. URIs can and often do
1506   appear almost “anywhere” in freeform human-readable text – e.g., typed or copied into E-mails,
1507   notes, documents, etc. Smart text editors often try to detect URIs on entry and automatically turn
1508   them into hyperlinks – but these heuristics can easily break because there is no unambiguous
1509   syntactic separation between the URI and its surrounding (particularly following) text. Suppose for
1510   example that a user types or copies this text into an E-mail:
1511             My site is https://example.com/index.html.
1512
         The trailing period (.) could be part of the URI, but in this case was probably intended to terminate
1513
       the English sentence. The user could try to “armor” the URI, like this:
                 See my site (https://example.com/index.html).
1514
1515
          But the close parenthesis, as well, could be part of the URI and be sucked into the link by a
1516
       “greedy” URI auto-recognizer, resulting in a broken link. A careful reader of Appendix C of the
1517
1518   1 For example: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/URI_(disambiguation)

1519
       32                                                                                               Anon.


1520   URI specification [5] might find the recommendation to delimit URIs with angle brackets <> – but
1521   rather few people seem to be aware of this recommendation in practice, let alone are following it.
1522
       F.3.3 Matchertext resource identifiers (MRIs). Given how commonly URIs are embedded in both
1523
       freeform human-readable text as well as other machine-readable syntaxes of all kinds, we suggest
1524
       that a more useful and ambitious potential evolution would make URI syntax self-delimiting. In
1525
       particular, let us consider an alternative potential URI syntax in which we surround the URI’s
1526
       body – everything after the scheme name – with square brackets instead of separating it from the
1527
       scheme name with a colon. Thus, http://my.site/ becomes http[//my.site/]. This alternate
1528
       syntax uses only characters that are already used (and reserved) in current URI syntax, and it
1529
       remains readily recognizable in freeform embedded contexts, but now the end can always be found
1530
       unambiguously with no heuristic guessing.
1531
          Let’s call this new syntax a matchertext resource identifier or MRI. Since MRI syntax is distinct
1532
       and not readily confused with traditional URIs, it could enforce the rule that all URI body content
1533
       within the brackets must be matchertext – i.e., that unmatched matchers in the body must be
1534
       percent-encoded – for verbatim embedding of other syntaxes (or other MRIs) in the body. Just as
1535
       IRIs [15] liberalized URI syntax while preserving backward compatibility by defining automatic
1536
       conversions in both directions, MRI syntax could similarly be converted automatically to or from
1537
       traditional URI and IRI syntax.
1538
          Assume that MRI syntax includes the extensions discussed at the start of this appendix – in
1539
       particular the rule that a square bracket sequence [𝑚] nested within the URI body protects the
1540
       embedded matchertext 𝑚 from percent-encoding in the outer context. With this syntax, MRIs
1541
       cleanly nest with no escaping needed, not even to introduce a matchertext embedding context. An
1542
       embedded MRI appearing in a path or query string component of a host MRI never need be escaped,
1543
       for example, as illustrated by the examples in fig. 5, where traditional URI syntax must instead
1544
       escape the colon (:) and slash (/) characters of the embedded URI as %3A and %2F, respectively.
1545

                          http://search.engine/linksto?site=http%3A%2F%2Fmy.site%2F&results=50
1546
            URI syntax:
1547
            MRI syntax:   http[//search.engine/linksto?site=http[//my.site/]&results=50]
1548
1549        URI syntax:   http://historical.archive/get?site=http%3A%2F%2Fmy.site%2F&year=1998
1550        MRI syntax:   http[//historical.archive/get?site=http[//my.site/]&year=1998]
1551
1552   Fig. 5. Example queries containing embedded resource identifiers in URI and MRI syntax for comparison.
1553
1554     Moreover, MRI syntax could potentially be simpler than traditional URI syntax, because complex
1555   and rarely-used sub-syntaxes such as IPv4 and IPv6 addresses could be “broken out” of the main
1556   MRI syntax and handled instead as embedded MRIs in the host MRI’s authority field. For example,
1557   the URI ‘http://1.2.3.4:80/’ would become the 2-level MRI ‘http[//ip4[1.2.3.4]:80/]’, and
1558   the URI ‘http://[1234::abcd]:80/’ would become the MRI ‘http[//ip6[1234::abcd]:80/]’.
1559   The MRI host field syntax thus needs to know only about domain names or nested MRIs, and not
1560   about IP address syntax.
1561
1562   G    Matchertext string interpolation
1563   Section 4 focuses on the problem of hosting arbitrary matchertext strings, verbatim, while eliminat-
1564   ing the need for escaping. It thus assumes that the semantic value of a string literal (the “output”
1565   from scanning the literal) should ideally be identical to and unmodified from the literal’s “input”
1566   (the “input” character sequence between the literal’s delimiters) – and the matchertext discipline
1567   indeed makes this goal achievable.
1568
       Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                                 33


1569       The string-literal syntax in many programming and scripting languages, however, often and
1570   increasingly supports string interpolation: the substitution of strings residing in variables, function
1571   parameters, or even computed by arbitrary host-language expressions, to be substituted into explicit
1572   “holes” in an otherwise-verbatim string literal. If name is a variable containing the string ‘Bob’, for
1573   example, then to construct the string ‘Hi Bob’, instead of manual concatenation via an expression
1574   like "Hi "+name, one may instead write f'Hi {name}' in Python, 'Hi ${name}' in JavaScript,
1575   "Hi #{name}" in Ruby, "Hi \(name)" in Swift, or just "Hi $name" in many shells and scripting
1576   languages such as Bash, Perl, and PHP.
1577       String interpolation extends the functional role of string literals from verbatim string expression
1578   to template-based string processing: automating the concatenation of verbatim and computed
1579   strings to form a result. It may at first appear that matchertext hosting and string interpolation
1580   are incompatible, since our matchertext goal has mostly been to avoid modifying strings we wish
1581   to express verbatim, while string interpolation’s goal is precisely to modify a template string by
1582   filling holes in well-defined ways. Indeed, if we are to have any way to specify a hole to be filled in
1583   a template, allowing that hole to be anywhere in the string, then it appears we must make some
1584   character sequences in the template sensitive, and thus forbidden or escaped in verbatim text (e.g.,
1585   the ‘$’ that introduces interpolated variable names in many scripting languages).
1586       There is nevertheless a different role that matchertext might usefully play in conjunction with
1587   string interpolation: namely defining and enforcing a hierarchical notion of structural integrity dur-
1588   ing interpolation. This alternative role could be especially important for security, where traditional
1589   string interpolation based on structure-oblivious concatenation has been at least partly responsible
1590   for an enormous number of critical security bugs historically, starting with the quintessential SQL
1591   injection attack [11]. We therefore propose below potential matchertext-aware extensions that
1592   support string interpolation while ensuring structural integrity.
1593
1594   G.1   Interpolation in matchertext literals
1595   We suggest a potential string-interpolation extension to the cross-language matchertext literal
1596   syntax described in section 4.2.1. An interpolating matchertext literal has the form M𝑑"(𝑚)",
1597   M𝑑"[𝑚]", or M𝑑"{𝑚}", where 𝑑 is a delimiter string consisting solely of one or more strictly-nested
1598   matcher pairs specifying the delimiters to be used to express holes or antiquotations within the literal.
1599   In this syntax, for example, several equivalent ways to express the interpolation example above
1600   would be M{}"(Hi {name})", M[]"{Hi [name]}", M()"(Hi (name))", M{{}}"[Hi {{name}}]",
1601   or M([{}])"[Hi ([{name}])]".
1602       The intent of this string-interpolation syntax goes beyond merely “filling in holes” in a template,
1603   however. The expectation is that not just the template itself, but also all of the interpolated hole-
1604   filling strings, must be matchertext-compliant: otherwise the interpolation processing yields some
1605   error whose reporting and handling is language-dependent. If the variable name contains the non-
1606   matchertext string ‘Eve(’, for example, then the interpolation in the above example fails with an
1607   error, and in particular does not just “blindly” use concatenation to produce the string ‘Hi Eve(’.
1608       Enforcing matchertext discipline on both the template and the interpolated strings ensures
1609   that the result is valid matchertext, and more generally ensures that interpolated strings cannot
1610   compromise the hierarchical structure of the template. This property can be useful as a security
1611   measure, since a vast number of critical SQL injection attacks and other input-validation attacks,
1612   historically, have relied on violating the structure of an interpolated template. In many SQL injection
1613   attacks, for example, an insufficiently-constrained user-entered string interpolated into an SQL
1614   query between quotes might contain a quote mark that gets interpreted as an “early” close quote
1615   followed by arbitrary attack code that gets executed as SQL code on the server side. If the receiving
1616   language, here SQL, also delimits each hole with matchers, as in a matchertext literal M'(. . . )',
1617
       34                                                                                              Anon.


1618   it ends the value by matcher balance rather than at a quote, so a quote in the value stays data.
1619   Using matchertext literals and interpolation instead of conventional literals in both languages could
1620   thus provide a layer of protection against such attacks below and independent of the complex
1621   language-dependent parsing and string-handling code. In essence, matchertext interpolation could
1622   be viewed as “microsegmentation of text-based formats”, analogous to the already-accepted best
1623   practice of microsegmentation of networks.
1624      Error handling is necessarily language-dependent, of course, and we expect should match the
1625   conventions of a given language. Languages like Java that support exception handling might use
1626   those to handle matchertext interpolation errors, for example. We might envision future strongly-
1627   typed languages having a matchertext type representing a string that is statically known to be
1628   valid matchertext, either as a result of how it was produced or by an explicit check for example.
1629      In some contexts it may be undesirable or impossible for a matchertext interpolation error to affect
1630   control flow. An alternative in such cases might be for matchertext interpolation to replace any non-
1631   matchertext strings with a single Unicode replacement character (U+FFFD), whose standardized
1632   purpose is to serve as an explicit placeholder for something invalid or non-representable. This
1633   approach makes interpolation errors “silent”, while at least ensuring that the interpolated result is
1634   still valid matchertext, preserves the template’s hierarchical structure, and that the interpolated
1635   replacement character is unlikely to be interpreted as useful “code” an attacker might make use of
1636   in practically any conceivable language.
1637
1638   G.2   Lower-case literal variants
1639   If the matchertext literals of section 4.2.1 become a cross-language standard, each language decides
1640   the meaning, if any, of variants like the lower-case m"𝑚". Such language-specific choices include:
1641   (a) no lower-case variant (syntax error); (b) m"(𝑚)" is equivalent to M"(𝑚)"; i.e., the M is simply
1642   case-insensitive; (c) m"𝑚" without a matcher pair around the content 𝑚 might be a constrained,
1643   shorthand syntax usable only for matchertext strings 𝑚 that contain no double-quotes outside of
1644   matcher pairs; or (d) m"𝑚" might be a “hybrid” syntax in which the host language’s usual escaping
1645   mechanisms are active outside of matcher pairs within the embedded string, hence allowing any
1646   matchertext string to be represented at the cost of allowing the host language’s escaping to “leak”
1647   into the outermost context of the embedded string. Options (a) and (b) appear conceptually simpler
1648   and cleaner, with (c) and (d) mentioned mainly as potential alternatives that could optimize different
1649   pragmatic tradeoffs. Appendix G.3 applies option (d) to interpolation.
1650
1651   G.3   Hybrid matchertext interpolation
1652   The matchertext interpolation syntax of appendix G.1 is suggested as one that appears likely
1653   backward-compatible with a large number of existing languages, and could help provide some cross-
1654   language consistency if adopted. Many languages already have their own well-defined interpolation
1655   syntax, however, sometimes related to the host language’s normal escaping syntax as in Swift’s
1656   interpolation escapes like \(name) in string literals. Since a template for interpolation is intended
1657   for modification anyway, escapes or other “sensitive” characters in such templates are unavoidable,
1658   so avoiding them is arguably less important than when using literals for verbatim embedding.
1659      As a result, there may be a pragmatic argument for languages to offer hybrid matchertext
1660   interpolation syntax, which enforces the matchertext structural discipline (e.g., for security), but
1661   maintains the host language’s normal escaping and interpolation syntax. In Python, for example,
1662   an extension might support syntax like m'Hi {name}', where exactly the same interpolation and
1663   escaping syntax apply within the quotes as with Python’s existing f'Hi {name}' syntax – except
1664   that the matchertext syntax ensures that the template, all interpolated strings, and the output are
1665   all valid matchertext.
1666
       Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                                35


1667   H     A compiler grammar for matchertext
1668
       Realizing the syntactic extensions of section 4 in an existing compiler reduces to a single requirement:
1669
       the additions must form a conservative extension of the language, under which every previously
1670
       valid program stays valid and keeps its meaning. Only a conservative extension can be adopted
1671
       incrementally, enabled behind a configuration flag without endangering existing code, the backward
1672
       compatibility that section 4 identifies as essential to adoption. The general technique is to guard
1673
       each new form with a marker the old grammar could never accept, so the extension fires only on
1674
       input the language previously rejected. We give grammar rules of this kind for the two hosting
1675
       extensions of section 4.2 in turn, first the matchertext literal and then, more briefly, the matchertext
1676
       escape.
1677
1678   H.1    Matchertext-literal grammar
1679
       We now cast the matchertext literal of section 4.2.1 as concrete grammar rules that a C-like language
1680
       could fold into its lexer.
1681
          We assume the target language already parses ordinary string literals with a rule of the general
1682
       shape:
1683                                  content ::= ...
1684                                delimiter ::= "
1685                                    string ::= delimiter content delimiter
1686
       The delimiter is shown here as a double quote, but any string delimiter the language already uses
       would serve equally well, for instance ', ", """, ''', or a backtick.
1687

          The proposed form is M𝑑"𝑜 . . . 𝑐", an ordinary string literal carrying a mandatory M prefix and
1688

       an optional specifier 𝑑. Its content 𝑜 . . . 𝑐 is itself wrapped in a matcher pair, 𝑜 one of (, [, { and
1689
1690
       𝑐 its matching close. That wrapping is the crux: the processor finds the literal’s end by matcher
1691
       balance, at the 𝑐 closing the opening 𝑜 (theorem 2), not at the first quote it meets inside, so the
1692
       content may hold any character, quotes included, as long as its matchers balance. This is exactly
1693
       the matchertext discipline, and theorem 1 then guarantees the content embeds verbatim without
1694
       escaping. The optional 𝑑, one or more strictly nested matcher pairs, names the pair reserved for
1695
       interpolation holes or antiquotations inside the literal (appendix G), so a template can mark its
       holes unambiguously. The M prefix keeps the extension conservative in languages whose grammars
1696
1697
       reject an identifier directly before a quote, such as Python, Go, and Java, and Rust 2021, which
1698
       reserves all such prefixes for future use. Other languages need more care. In C and C++, a macro
       named M can make M". . . " valid today, the same incompatibility that C++11 accepted for raw-string
1699

       prefixes such as R. Scala reads any identifier before a quote as a string interpolator, and JavaScript
1700
1701
       reads an identifier before a backtick as a tagged template. Such languages need a marker that their
       grammar rejects, as CHICKEN Scheme does with #M (section 6).
1702
1703
          We first define the matchertext symbols used (prefixed with MT):
1704
1705                  MT _prefix     ::=   M
1706                      MT _d      ::=   (MT _d) | [MT _d] | {MT _d} | 𝜖
1707                  MT _string     ::=   delimiter ( MT _body ) delimiter
1708                                   |   delimiter { MT _body } delimiter
1709                                   |   delimiter [ MT _body ] delimiter
1710                   MT _body      ::=   MT _char MT _body | ( MT _body ) MT _body
1711                                   |   [ MT _body ] MT _body | { MT _body } MT _body | 𝜖
1712                    MT _char     ::=   any character except ( ) [ ] { }
1713   MT_body is the matchertext language 𝐿 of section 3.1 in the standard configuration. It replaces the
1714   ordinary content, so quotes and escapes inside it have no meaning to the host.
1715
       36                                                                                               Anon.


1716     We then introduce the extended rule string_ext and use it wherever the grammar previously
1717   accepted a string. Its first alternative is the unchanged string rule, so every existing literal parses
1718   exactly as before, and its remaining alternatives add the matchertext forms:
1719
                                  string_ext   ::= string
1720
                                                 | MT _prefix MT _d MT _string
1721
1722      We also give the same rules in LL(1) form, so a predictive parser can select each alternative from
1723   one token of lookahead. Here MT_string omits the leading delimiter, which MT_content supplies,
1724   letting the parser decide as soon as it sees the opening quote or an opening matcher after the M:
1725                            string_ext     ::=   string | MT _prefix MT _content
1726                           MT _content     ::=   MT _d delimiter MT _string
1727                                 MT _d     ::=   ( MT _d ) | [ MT _d ]
1728                                             |   { MT _d } | 𝜖
1729                             MT _string    ::=   ( MT _body ) delimiter
1730                                             |   { MT _body } delimiter
1731                                             |   [ MT _body ] delimiter
1732
1733   H.2    Matchertext-escape grammar
1734   The matchertext escape asks less of the grammar than a new literal form, at least for C-like
1735   languages, because the property a host must enforce inside the escape, that matchers balance,
1736   is one these languages already enforce throughout their ordinary syntax. The expression, block,
1737   and argument-list grammars of C, C++, Rust, Java, Python, and their relatives all require every
1738   (, [, and { to be matched for a program to compile at all, so at the structural level their code is
1739   mostly matchertext already. C and C++ have two exceptions outside literals and comments. The
1740   preprocessor runs before the parser, so #define BEGIN { or two #if branches that each open
1741   a { leave matchers unmatched in the source text. Digraphs spell brackets with other characters,
1742   so a<:0] compiles but is not matchertext. Code that uses either cannot be embedded verbatim
1743   as matchertext. Apart from these, the only contexts in which these languages admit unmatched
1744   matchers are the opaque ones, string and character literals and comments, whose contents the
1745   compiler does not otherwise interpret.
1746      Those contexts are also the ones backward compatibility forbids us to constrain for existing,
1747   non-embedded code, so a host does not tighten them globally. It instead introduces a bracketed
1748   embedding region within them, such as the \[𝑚] escape of section 4.2.2, inside which two rules
1749   apply, following the general hosting principle of section 4: the host disables its own escaping and
1750   other transformations, and locates the region’s end by matcher balance (theorem 2) rather than
1751   by its usual literal or comment terminator. Because the surrounding code already balances its
1752   matchers, this region composes cleanly with it, and the grammar change a C-like host needs is
1753   correspondingly small: the discipline it must impose inside an embedding is the one it already
1754   imposes everywhere else.
1755
1756   I    Matchertext literals in Go: experiment details
1757   The patch of section 6.2 adds M"(. . . )", M"[. . . ]", and M"{. . . }" to cmd/compile/internal/syntax,
1758   go/scanner, and go/constant. The content of such a literal is its value verbatim: it has no escapes,
1759   and unlike in Go’s backquoted raw strings its carriage returns are kept. The scanner rejects a literal
1760   whose content is not matchertext, or whose closing matcher no quote follows.
1761      The rewriting tool converts an interpreted literal ". . . " only if the literal has a backslash, its
1762   source text and its value are matchertext, and its value is valid UTF-8 with no NUL, byte-order mark,
1763   or control character other than line feed and tab. It leaves import paths and struct tags unchanged,
1764
       Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                                            37


1765   which the compiler unquotes itself, and skips testdata and vendor directories and files that use
1766   cgo. Unlike the corpus rewriting of section 7.1, which normalizes control characters, it therefore
1767   preserves every value exactly and leaves literals of control characters or binary data as they are.
1768      Table 7 lists the four repositories, pinned to the commits tested. Each was tested with
1769   go test -short ./... three times: with stock Go, with the patched toolchain on the unchanged
1770   code, and with the patched toolchain after rewriting the repository’s own code. Dependencies came
1771   unchanged from the module cache, so the patched toolchain also compiled them unmodified. The
1772   pass, fail, and skip outcome of every package was identical across the three runs. The 88 toothpicks
1773   left in the rewritten literals are backslashes of the value itself, written by \\ or another escape that
1774   decodes to a backslash. The artifact includes the patch, the tool, the script, and these results.
1775
1776          Repository (commit)            Packages   With tests   Files changed   Literals rewritten    Toothpicks
1777          cockroachdb/uniseg (f77ce19)          1            1               8                7,739    24,831 → 6
1778          golang/text (6070ac3)                63          48              132                3,042    6,470 → 40
1779          golang/net (3de643d)                 41          36               87                  924     1,630 → 9
              golang/tools (588ada3)              217         157              446                2,692    4,731 → 33
1780
              Total                               322         242              673               14,397   37,662 → 88

       Table 7. Go test outcomes before and after rewriting: packages, packages with tests (all passing in all three
       runs), files changed, literals rewritten, and their toothpicks before and after.

       J     Matchertext configuration variations
1788   Even if adequately well-justified, we cannot expect the standard matchertext configuration of
1789   section 3.2 to be a perfect or painless fit for all situations in which string embedding is useful.
1790   Including any matcher pair in Π has the cost of requiring those matchers to be escaped in string
1791   literals and comments, for example, as section 5 details. There may be legitimate or even unavoidable
1792   reasons to use other matchertext configurations in some cases, keeping in mind that doing so
1793   reduces interlanguage embedding compatibility.
1794      In general, deviations from the standard matchertext configuration can be either tightening (more
1795   restrictive), loosening (less restrictive), or a combination.
1796
1797   J.1    Tightening variations
1798   A matchertext configuration (Σ′, Π ′ ) is a tightening of the standard matchertext configuration
1799   (Σ, Π) if it only removes characters from the alphabet (Σ′ ⊆ Σ) and/or makes additional matcher
1800   pairs sensitive (Π ′ ⊇ Π), where each added pair (𝑜, 𝑐) ∈ Π ′ \ Π consists of two characters that
1801   are nonmatchers in the standard configuration (𝑜, 𝑐 ∈ 𝑁 ). A string in the tightened matchertext
1802   configuration may then be copied verbatim to an embedding context expecting the standard
1803   matchertext configuration, but not necessarily in the other direction: by induction on its derivation,
1804   each nesting step with a standard pair is a nesting step in 𝐿, and each nesting step 𝑜 ||𝑚||𝑐 with an
1805   added pair concatenates the nonmatchers 𝑜 and 𝑐 around 𝑚 ∈ 𝐿, which stays in 𝐿 by lemma 1. The
1806   restriction matters: adding a pair such as ( with ], whose characters already match other characters,
1807   would admit (], which the standard configuration rejects.
1808      As appendix F.2 details, uniform resource identifiers (URIs) [5] traditionally allow only graphical
1809   characters – and no spaces or control codes for example – in order to make them manually
1810   transcribable. To serve this transcribability purpose, significant spaces and control codes must not
1811   appear anywhere in a URI, even in an embedded matchertext substring. Thus, URIs may represent
1812   a justifiable use-case for an alternate matchertext configuration that removes the non-graphical
1813
       38                                                                                             Anon.


1814   characters from the alphabet. This would unfortunately mean that a string cannot, in general, be
1815   copied from a standard matchertext language into a matchertext URI without transformation (i.e.,
1816   escaping spaces and control codes).
1817
1818   J.2   Loosening variations
1819   A matchertext configuration (Σ′, Π ′ ) is a loosening of the standard matchertext configuration (Σ, Π)
1820   if it only adds characters to the alphabet (Σ′ ⊇ Σ) and/or removes sensitive matcher pairs (Π ′ ⊆ Π).
1821   A string in the standard matchertext configuration may be copied verbatim to an embedding context
1822   supporting the loosened matchertext configuration, but not necessarily in the other direction.
1823       A loosened matchertext configuration might be justified, for example, if it is deemed critical to
1824   embed strings in some language 𝐿𝑒 that frequently makes unmatched uses of some ASCII matchers,
1825   and the pain of escaping or otherwise adapting that syntax is deemed too great.
1826       Mathematical notation, for example, sometimes uses “mismatched” parentheses and square
1827   brackets to represent half-open/half-closed intervals. That is, [0, 1) typically means any real number
1828   𝑟 greater than or equal to zero but strictly less than one (0 ≤ 𝑟 < 1). A machine-readable language
1829   making frequent use of this mathematical notation might be considered too painful to embed in a
1830   standard matchertext configuration, and therefore might “demand” a looser configuration in which
1831   perhaps only the curly braces are sensitive as matcher pairs.
1832       This example seems fairly hypothetical, however, as extremely few machine-readable languages
1833   appear to support this mathematical half-open/half-closed interval notation anyway. Languages
1834   that do support some form of half-open/half-closed syntax often do so with other, more matchertext-
1835   friendly notation. Swift, for example, supports half-open range syntax like 1..<4 for the sequence
1836   of integers starting from and including 1, up to but not including 4 [4]. This syntax is perfectly
1837   compatible with the standard matchertext configuration because it uses the mathematical inequality
1838   operators, rather than unmatched matchers, to express the range’s open upper endpoint.
1839
1840   K     Regular Expression Syntax
1841   Despite being a “small” syntax for the special purpose of matching patterns in strings, regular
1842   expressions (REs) and their use are complex enough in practice that multiple entire books have been
1843   written about them [18, 22, 24]. Two regular expression syntaxes were standardized by POSIX [32],
1844   while the Perl language and the Perl Compatible Regular Expressions (PCRE) library it inspired
1845   define advanced syntax that has become popular in numerous other languages and applications
1846   (Perl, PCRE).
1847      In filling their basic role of matching patterns in text, REs must inherently embed strings
1848   comprising the patterns to be matched – and those embedded strings can be in any syntax. Thus,
1849   being able to host embedded strings of any language with minimal obfuscation in principle facilitates
1850   an RE’s basic pattern-matching role.
1851      Since the most common RE syntax uses backslash escapes similar to those in C-like languages,
1852   the same matchertext escape extensions, such as \[𝑚], could work for REs. Because of the large
1853   number of punctuation characters that are sensitive in REs, however, some popular RE syntaxes
1854   such as PCRE guarantee the rule that if a backslash “is followed by a character that is not a number
1855   or a letter, it takes away any special meaning that character may have” (PCRE). This way, a user can
1856   just conservatively escape all literal punctuation appearing in an RE, instead of remembering which
1857   punctuation must be escaped. Preserving this rule may suggest a longer, letter-based matchertext
1858   escape sequence such as \m[𝑚].
1859      Another alternative would be to use some non-backslash-escape syntax, such as {{𝑚}}. This
1860   alternative syntax uses the same curly braces that REs already commonly use for repetition quanti-
1861   fiers like 𝑐{1,3}, but in a syntactically non-conflicting fashion since the inner braces cannot be
1862
       Matchertext: Towards Verbatim Interlanguage Embedding                                                39


1863   mistaken for repetition quantifiers. With this alternative syntax, the pathological “leaning toothpick
1864   syndrome” example RE, matching the double-backslash \\ in a UNC name (see section 2), becomes
1865   the more readable RE {{\\}} (leaning toothpicks). Embedding this RE in a C-like string literal with
1866   matchertext extensions in turn becomes M"({{\\}})" or "\[{{\\}}]", for a more manageable
1867   two or three leaning toothpicks, in contrast with the traditionally-required eight in "\\\\\\\\".
1868
1869   K.1   Embedding regular expressions
1870   Typical regular expression (RE) syntax is C-like in terms of using backslashes to escape sensitive
1871   punctuation characters within text to be matched. Similar escape sequences like \o and \c for
1872   unmatched matchers could therefore be introduced as section 5.1 discusses.
1873      One complication is that the popular PCRE syntax already uses \o{𝑛} for character escapes
1874   with octal numeric value 𝑛 (PCRE). This octal-escape usage of \o technically does not conflict
1875   syntactically with \o{}, however, since the 𝑛 in an octal escape cannot be the empty string.
1876      PCRE syntax also offers \c𝑥 as a way to enter control characters, by flipping bit 6 of ASCII
1877   character 𝑥. This is a syntactic conflict with the proposed matchertext escapes, but perhaps a
1878   tolerable one. The sequence \c( would constitute a bizarre and unlikely way to express a simple
1879   literal letter ‘h’, and \c{ would be a strange synonym for a semicolon ‘;’ – neither of which need
1880   escaping at all. The sequence \c[ might be slightly more likely to see use to express the ASCII
1881   escape (ESC) control code (hex 1B) – but PCRE already provides the more-concise and obvious
1882   sequence \e to express this control code.
1883
       K.1.1 Character classes. In POSIX syntax, backslash escapes are disabled in bracketed RE character
1884
       class notation like [a-z0-9], and a ] closes the class unless it comes first. The matchertext discipline
1885
       does not present a problem when expressing a character class containing both matchers of a
1886
       pair. For example, the character class [][(){}] matches any matcher character, while [^][]
1887
       matches anything but a square bracket. Including just one unmatched matcher in a character
1888
       class becomes less convenient, however. A slightly-cumbersome workaround is simply to shift
1889
       unmatched matchers outside the character class: e.g., [a-z{] might be rewritten as ([a-z]|\o{}).
1890
          A more-appealing syntactic extension might be to introduce the rule that a less-than character <
1891
       in a character class, when immediately surrounded by a pair of matchers, “selects” only the open
1892
       matcher for literal inclusion. The example above therefore becomes [a-z{<}]. A greater-than
1893
       character > between a matcher pair similarly selects only the close matcher: [^[>]] matches
1894
       anything but a close bracket. Under this rule, the RE parser reads each such three-character unit
1895
       before it looks for the end of the class, so the class ends at the final bracket. The rule changes the
1896
       meaning of existing classes that contain such a unit: today [a-z{<}] also matches < and }. One
1897
       might view the < or > character either as a matchertext-insensitive angle-bracket “standing in” for
1898
       the desired sensitive matcher, or as an arrow “pointing” left or right to the desired matcher.
